items.title: AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
items.summary: Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java. The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges . The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015. A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both are fixed in Nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, which F5 released along with fixes for eight other vulnerabilities. Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can be chained with any of those flaws to gain root privileges on the server. The company has dubbed the collection nginx2root . In their tests the exploit chain escaped a Docker container running Nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. The kernel flaw has existed since Linux 4.15, released in 2018, and has no CVE or patch so the company is withholding details until distributions can ship a fix. The exposure of web servers on the internet is vast with the Shodan search engine showing 56.7 million hosts running Nginx, and 98.9% of those that disclose their version report one in the vulnerable range. F5 recommends updating immediately or disabling HTTP/2 on affected ports, which blocks the two most severe flaws but not Xint’s other findings — CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425 — which are in other components. The CVE-2026-123007 flaw was reported to F5 by researchers from Rapid7 , Wiz , Xint, and Ikotas Labs , while CVE-2026-123633, dubbed Drainbreak, was discovered and reported by researchers from Metnir , Wiz, and Xint. Only Rapid7 senior principal security researcher Stephen Fewer doesn’t mention AI in his write-up. The other four teams used AI agents and harnesses, with Xint’s CEO Brian Pak saying that his team’s platform scanned “50,000 lines of code in just 90 minutes” to surface “a critical vulnerability that gave an unauthenticated user a RCE path — essentially an internet breaker.” Exploitation is likely No one has exploited either flaw in the wild yet, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s assessment of both CVEs, but every research team built working exploits, and two describe the flaws as readily exploitable. Xint called CVE-2026-123007 highly exploitable, saying an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port was enough to corrupt the send window, disclose addresses, and execute commands, and validated the attack over public IPs on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent traffic. Metnir ran its exploit for CVE-2026-123633 with ASLR enabled, taking about 10 minutes, nearly all of it spent on defeating memory layout randomization, and reproduced the use-after-free in OpenResty, crashing the shipped binaries of Kong, Apache APISIX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and community ingress-nginx, all of which enable HTTP/2 by default. Rapid7’s Fewer calculated that running his exploit requires transmitting roughly 128GB of HTTP/2 data to the target. That takes about two minutes on a 10Gbit/s network and 17 minutes on 1Gbit/s. The technique also relies on a memory-copy routine in glibc that is used only on CPUs with AVX-512 extensions, but these are common on servers. “Exploitation is by no means a walk in the park, as the vulnerable systems must be directly exposed to the internet with no WAF or CDN terminating HTTP/2,” Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, told CSO. “Memory corruption can also be tricky, as an effective exploit must properly groom and shape the memory heap and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configuration variants. And when the system is internet-facing and under load, exploitation can cause more crashes than successful code execution.” Patch and check what you’re actually running Nginx Plus users should also update to 37.3.0.1 on the newer release line or 37.0.8.1 on the 37.0 line. The older R33 through R36 release line will never receive a fix because those versions have reached the end of technical support. Disabling HTTP/2 comes with costs, as services that depend on it, such as native gRPC, stop working. Xint’s other three flaws require specific configurations. The resolver flaw affects setups that pick their backend per request and use the mirror directive, the HTTP/3 flaw affects QUIC listeners, and the mail proxy flaw affects deployments that use proxy on with auth_http . Xint published per-flaw mitigations in its technical write-up. For the accompanying Linux flaw, until a kernel patch is released, administrators who don’t use SCTP can block the module from loading by adding install sctp /bin/false to a file under /etc/modprobe.d . Administrators should also investigate unexpected Nginx worker crashes or commands launched by Nginx workers, Wiz noted. “The real risk with this nginx bug isn’t the 11 years it went unnoticed, it’s how many teams will think they’ve patched when they haven’t,” Daniel Shechter, co-founder and CEO of Miggo Security, told CSO. “The version number can be wrong because distros backport fixes without changing it, a reload doesn’t swap out the running code, and the attack happens in HTTP/2 traffic that WAFs and access logs never see. If you can’t prove the fix is actually running, assume you’re still exposed.”
items.summary_html:
Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both are fixed in Nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, which F5 released along with fixes for eight other vulnerabilities.

Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can be chained with any of those flaws to gain root privileges on the server. The company has dubbed the collection nginx2root.

In their tests the exploit chain escaped a Docker container running Nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. The kernel flaw has existed since Linux 4.15, released in 2018, and has no CVE or patch so the company is withholding details until distributions can ship a fix.

The exposure of web servers on the internet is vast with the Shodan search engine showing 56.7 million hosts running Nginx, and 98.9% of those that disclose their version report one in the vulnerable range. F5 recommends updating immediately or disabling HTTP/2 on affected ports, which blocks the two most severe flaws but not Xint’s other findings — CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425 — which are in other components.

The CVE-2026-123007 flaw was reported to F5 by researchers from Rapid7, Wiz, Xint, and Ikotas Labs, while CVE-2026-123633, dubbed Drainbreak, was discovered and reported by researchers from Metnir, Wiz, and Xint. Only Rapid7 senior principal security researcher Stephen Fewer doesn’t mention AI in his write-up. The other four teams used AI agents and harnesses, with Xint’s CEO Brian Pak saying that his team’s platform scanned “50,000 lines of code in just 90 minutes” to surface “a critical vulnerability that gave an unauthenticated user a RCE path — essentially an internet breaker.”

Exploitation is likely

No one has exploited either flaw in the wild yet, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s assessment of both CVEs, but every research team built working exploits, and two describe the flaws as readily exploitable.

Xint called CVE-2026-123007 highly exploitable, saying an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port was enough to corrupt the send window, disclose addresses, and execute commands, and validated the attack over public IPs on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent traffic.

Metnir ran its exploit for CVE-2026-123633 with ASLR enabled, taking about 10 minutes, nearly all of it spent on defeating memory layout randomization, and reproduced the use-after-free in OpenResty, crashing the shipped binaries of Kong, Apache APISIX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and community ingress-nginx, all of which enable HTTP/2 by default.

Rapid7’s Fewer calculated that running his exploit requires transmitting roughly 128GB of HTTP/2 data to the target. That takes about two minutes on a 10Gbit/s network and 17 minutes on 1Gbit/s. The technique also relies on a memory-copy routine in glibc that is used only on CPUs with AVX-512 extensions, but these are common on servers.

“Exploitation is by no means a walk in the park, as the vulnerable systems must be directly exposed to the internet with no WAF or CDN terminating HTTP/2,” Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, told CSO. “Memory corruption can also be tricky, as an effective exploit must properly groom and shape the memory heap and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configuration variants. And when the system is internet-facing and under load, exploitation can cause more crashes than successful code execution.”

Patch and check what you’re actually running

Nginx Plus users should also update to 37.3.0.1 on the newer release line or 37.0.8.1 on the 37.0 line. The older R33 through R36 release line will never receive a fix because those versions have reached the end of technical support.

Disabling HTTP/2 comes with costs, as services that depend on it, such as native gRPC, stop working. Xint’s other three flaws require specific configurations. The resolver flaw affects setups that pick their backend per request and use the mirror directive, the HTTP/3 flaw affects QUIC listeners, and the mail proxy flaw affects deployments that use proxy on with auth_http. Xint published per-flaw mitigations in its technical write-up.

For the accompanying Linux flaw, until a kernel patch is released, administrators who don’t use SCTP can block the module from loading by adding install sctp /bin/false to a file under /etc/modprobe.d.

Administrators should also investigate unexpected Nginx worker crashes or commands launched by Nginx workers, Wiz noted.

“The real risk with this nginx bug isn’t the 11 years it went unnoticed, it’s how many teams will think they’ve patched when they haven’t,” Daniel Shechter, co-founder and CEO of Miggo Security, told CSO. “The version number can be wrong because distros backport fixes without changing it, a reload doesn’t swap out the running code, and the attack happens in HTTP/2 traffic that WAFs and access logs never see. If you can’t prove the fix is actually running, assume you’re still exposed.”

items.title: CDJapan’s Data Breach Is Far Bigger Than First Reported: 791,111 Customers and 360,538 Old Card Numbers
items.summary: CDJapan, the Tokyo shop that sells anime, J-pop and games to fans around the world, says its data breach is far bigger than it first reported. Its first notice, on 13 November, spoke of 285 cards entered over two days. The second report , published on 18 November after an outside forensics firm went through the systems, describes two separate thefts. One was a single copy of part of the customer database on 6 November: 360,538 card records from 2005 to 2018 and the contact details of 791,111 customers. The other was card-skimming code on the checkout page that ran for a week. Customers began sharing CDJapan’s emails on social media on 18 November. Some posts on Bluesky and X read it as every card used at CDJapan since 2005 being stolen together with its security code. The report doesn’t say that, and the difference decides what you need to do. Chapter 3 sorts it out by customer group. When we published, Anime News Network was the only news outlet we found covering the second report.

items.title: A new critical Java hole illustrates the enterprise IT visibility problem
items.summary: When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE). With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT. Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous. Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK x86-64 Base64 decoder that scores 9.2 in severity (Critical) under CVSS 4.0, Calif said. Oracle assigned it a lower rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1. Calif explained in its post describing the issue that Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. “It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” it wrote. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution.” It said that the corruption can be triggered by a string of just 64 “A” characters followed by a single equals sign (=); in older OpenJDK 17 versions, 128 “A” characters are required before the equals sign. “Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the internet,” Calif said. “But one of Java’s biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers’ behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.” Assessing the bug’s potential for exploit is complicated because triggering it requires a hardware accelerated decoding function that’s used on some x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. And fixing it requires patches from a lengthy list of vendors; just installing Tuesday’s patch from Oracle, which owns Java, is not going to do the trick. Potential damage ‘extreme’ Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, said the potential damage from an unpatched instance of exposed Java is extreme. “The researchers were able to read Java heap memory before they achieved code execution, so an attacker may be able to steal tokens, credentials, or keys from those systems. That access can remain useful even after the vulnerable server has been patched,” Kenney said. “Any unexplained crashes on an exposed system should lead to a review of what secrets were in memory and whether they need to be rotated.” But not every instance is vulnerable to this flaw. “The same Java application and version can be vulnerable on a newer x86 server and unaffected on older hardware because the faulty decoder only runs when AVX-512 is available,” he noted. “That makes a normal software inventory less useful than it usually is. CISOs need to know the Java distribution and version, the processor underneath it, and whether untrusted Base64 reaches the decoder. Installing a newer processor can expose an application that was safe on the server it replaced, without changing the application at all.” A further complication is that enterprises will also be running Java from a massive array of specialized vendors. “Oracle released a fix for its Java builds, but enterprises also run Java from Amazon, Eclipse, Microsoft, Red Hat, and Azul, along with runtimes buried inside commercial products and containers,” Kenney pointed out. “CISOs should start with identity systems and software-delivery infrastructure, identify the runtime each one is actually using, apply the appropriate vendor fix, and restart or rebuild the workload.” He also said that outbound connections need to be evaluated. “Researchers demonstrated that a Java program could be compromised by connecting to a malicious TLS server, even when it had no service exposed to the internet.” Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, agreed, pointing out, “the client-side exploit puts any Java process that connects to a malicious TLS server at risk: integrations, connectors, crawlers and batch jobs. Patch scopes built around internet-facing listeners will miss them.” Lack of visibility a big problem Mahapatra also stressed that many Java implementations can be hard to locate. “Your SBOM [software bill of materials] can’t see the real exposure. Whether a service is vulnerable depends on the silicon underneath as much as the JDK version,” he said. “The same container image is exploitable on an Ice Lake or Zen 4 node and safe on ARM or older hardware, and autoscaling can move it between the two. For once, the organizations that refreshed their hardware are the exposed ones.” But it is the lack of visibility that concerns practitioners the most. The Java hole “exposes a blind spot in how enterprises identify, prioritize and validate vulnerabilities,” said Raj Annaladasu , staff customer success engineer at Palo Alto Networks. “Enterprise teams invest heavily in application code review, dependency scanning, and secure coding practices. Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerabilities can originate below the application layer, inside the managed runtime itself.” “This is an important distinction: Java’s memory-safety abstractions do not protect an application from memory corruption originating inside a vulnerable native runtime implementation,” he said. “Applications may be using a standard Java API correctly while the underlying runtime implementation is vulnerable. This shifts the security boundary beyond application code and third-party dependencies to include the runtime, its implementation, and the hardware capabilities that influence execution.” This means, he said, that exploitability depends on multiple conditions coming together: an affected Java runtime, the relevant CPU instruction capabilities, the vulnerable execution path being enabled, and attacker-controlled input reaching the decoder. But, he pointed out, “one of the bigger challenges is discovering where Java is actually running. Runtime installations are often bundled inside third-party products, container images, appliances, custom runtime distributions, and application-specific directories. They may not appear as distinct entries in conventional software inventories. A clean application dependency scan or CMDB does not establish that the environment is free of vulnerable Java runtimes.” Java hides everywhere Given that there are going to be so many Java vendors, and so many hidden apps, at issue, the risk of a CISO missing a few is massive, noted Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “Java4Shell is a big deal because a single missed server with Java is all an attacker needs, allowing someone who never logs in to read its memory, including personal data, private keys, and tokens,” he said. “From there, the attacker can run code on the server. If that server is an identity system like Keycloak or PingFederate, the attacker now owns you.” And, he said, it’s highly unlikely that enterprise CISOs will catch all or most Java instances. “Will a CISO miss one? The odds say yes. Java hides everywhere. Each Java instance needs its own fix,” Dickson said. Its popularity is Java’s greatest weakness Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, said Java’s popularity is its biggest weakness. “Java runs the back office of corporate America: logins, code pipelines, ticketing, internal wikis,” he said. “Java4Shell lets an attacker who hasn’t even logged in take over some of the most sensitive of those systems by sending a short string of text. If your company runs Java on modern servers, and almost every large company does, you’re exposed until you patch.” He enumerated some examples: “Keycloak and PingFederate control who gets into your company. Jenkins and Artifactory build and store the software you ship. Jira and Confluence hold your roadmaps, incident notes and plenty of passwords people shouldn’t have pasted there,” he said. “Take over those and you aren’t breaking into one room. You’ve stolen the master key, the blueprints and the security guard’s notebook in one move.” He added, “Java programs that simply connect out to the wrong server can be compromised too. That last one means firewalls and perimeter controls don’t fully protect you.” However, he pointed out, “there’s one small mercy: the bug only fires on certain newer Intel and AMD chips. The catch is that those chips fill modern data centers and cloud fleets.”

“This is an important distinction: Java’s memory-safety abstractions do not protect an application from memory corruption originating inside a vulnerable native runtime implementation,” he said. “Applications may be using a standard Java API correctly while the underlying runtime implementation is vulnerable. This shifts the security boundary beyond application code and third-party dependencies to include the runtime, its implementation, and the hardware capabilities that influence execution.”

This means, he said, that exploitability depends on multiple conditions coming together: an affected Java runtime, the relevant CPU instruction capabilities, the vulnerable execution path being enabled, and attacker-controlled input reaching the decoder.

But, he pointed out, “one of the bigger challenges is discovering where Java is actually running. Runtime installations are often bundled inside third-party products, container images, appliances, custom runtime distributions, and application-specific directories. They may not appear as distinct entries in conventional software inventories. A clean application dependency scan or CMDB does not establish that the environment is free of vulnerable Java runtimes.”

Java hides everywhere

Given that there are going to be so many Java vendors, and so many hidden apps, at issue, the risk of a CISO missing a few is massive, noted Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research.

“Java4Shell is a big deal because a single missed server with Java is all an attacker needs, allowing someone who never logs in to read its memory, including personal data, private keys, and tokens,” he said. “From there, the attacker can run code on the server. If that server is an identity system like Keycloak or PingFederate, the attacker now owns you.”

And, he said, it’s highly unlikely that enterprise CISOs will catch all or most Java instances.

“Will a CISO miss one? The odds say yes. Java hides everywhere. Each Java instance needs its own fix,” Dickson said. 

Its popularity is Java’s greatest weakness

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, said Java’s popularity is its biggest weakness.

“Java runs the back office of corporate America: logins, code pipelines, ticketing, internal wikis,” he said. “Java4Shell lets an attacker who hasn’t even logged in take over some of the most sensitive of those systems by sending a short string of text. If your company runs Java on modern servers, and almost every large company does, you’re exposed until you patch.”

He enumerated some examples: “Keycloak and PingFederate control who gets into your company. Jenkins and Artifactory build and store the software you ship. Jira and Confluence hold your roadmaps, incident notes and plenty of passwords people shouldn’t have pasted there,” he said. “Take over those and you aren’t breaking into one room. You’ve stolen the master key, the blueprints and the security guard’s notebook in one move.”

He added, “Java programs that simply connect out to the wrong server can be compromised too. That last one means firewalls and perimeter controls don’t fully protect you.”

However, he pointed out, “there’s one small mercy: the bug only fires on certain newer Intel and AMD chips. The catch is that those chips fill modern data centers and cloud fleets.”

items.title: Apache Roller RCE Flaw CVE-2026-129448 Under Active Attack
items.summary: Attackers are exploiting a critical Apache Roller flaw that allows unauthenticated remote code execution, prompting urgent security updates. A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8), in Apache Roller could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. Apache Roller is an open-source blogging platform written in Java. According to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) the flaw is being actively exploited in attacks in the wild. The issue affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It stems from unsafe deserialization in the platform’s XML-RPC endpoint, which processes certain data before checking whether the requester is authenticated. An attacker doesn’t need valid credentials to reach this vulnerable code path. “Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.” reads the security notice published on the Apache mailing list. “This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.” The Apache project described the problem in its security notice published on the Apache mailing list : The maintainers explained that the XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester. This order of operations is the core security problem: the application processes attacker-controlled data before establishing whether the request should be trusted. The ASF also confirmed that the vulnerability is the same issue previously tracked as CVE-2026-82384 . That earlier advisory, published in September 2026, listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. The new notice expands the affected version range to include releases from 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, making it important for administrators not to rely solely on the scope of the earlier advisory. The project has explicitly confirmed exploitation in the wild, although it hasn’t disclosed technical details about the attacks, the threat actors involved, or the organizations being targeted. “This issue is being actively exploited. ” continues the notice. Security researcher n0mi1k is credited with discovering the vulnerability, while Matt Raible reported it to the project. The ASF recommends upgrading to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later. This release disables the vendor extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled. Organizations that can’t install the update immediately should apply one of the workarounds provided by the project. They can set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml , or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping. In either case, administrators must restart Apache Roller for the change to take effect. The experts warn that simply disabling XML-RPC through the administration interface doesn’t fully address the problem in older releases. The vulnerable code can deserialize the request before checking that configuration setting, leaving the application exposed even when administrators believe they have turned the feature off. The confirmed exploitation makes this more than a routine patching recommendation. Organizations running Apache Roller should identify every affected instance, check whether the XML-RPC endpoint is reachable, and prioritize the upgrade or the recommended workaround. Internet-facing systems deserve particular attention, but internal installations should not be overlooked: a server doesn’t need to be publicly accessible to become a useful target after an attacker gains access to an organization’s network. The ASF has also warned that disabling the feature through the administration interface alone won’t protect older installations: “Users who cannot upgrade right away should set “enabledForExtensions” to “false” in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the “/roller-services/xmlrpc” servlet mapping, and restart Roller.” concludes the advisory. “Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apache Roller)

Attackers are exploiting a critical Apache Roller flaw that allows unauthenticated remote code execution, prompting urgent security updates.

A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8), in Apache Roller could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. Apache Roller is an open-source blogging platform written in Java. According to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) the flaw is being actively exploited in attacks in the wild.

The issue affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It stems from unsafe deserialization in the platform’s XML-RPC endpoint, which processes certain data before checking whether the requester is authenticated. An attacker doesn’t need valid credentials to reach this vulnerable code path.

“Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.” reads the security notice published on the Apache mailing list. “This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.”

The Apache project described the problem in its security notice published on the Apache mailing list:

The maintainers explained that the XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester. This order of operations is the core security problem: the application processes attacker-controlled data before establishing whether the request should be trusted.

The ASF also confirmed that the vulnerability is the same issue previously tracked as CVE-2026-82384. That earlier advisory, published in September 2026, listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. The new notice expands the affected version range to include releases from 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, making it important for administrators not to rely solely on the scope of the earlier advisory.

The project has explicitly confirmed exploitation in the wild, although it hasn’t disclosed technical details about the attacks, the threat actors involved, or the organizations being targeted.

“This issue is being actively exploited.” continues the notice.

Security researcher n0mi1k is credited with discovering the vulnerability, while Matt Raible reported it to the project. The ASF recommends upgrading to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later. This release disables the vendor extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Organizations that can’t install the update immediately should apply one of the workarounds provided by the project. They can set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping. In either case, administrators must restart Apache Roller for the change to take effect.

The experts warn that simply disabling XML-RPC through the administration interface doesn’t fully address the problem in older releases. The vulnerable code can deserialize the request before checking that configuration setting, leaving the application exposed even when administrators believe they have turned the feature off.

The confirmed exploitation makes this more than a routine patching recommendation. Organizations running Apache Roller should identify every affected instance, check whether the XML-RPC endpoint is reachable, and prioritize the upgrade or the recommended workaround. Internet-facing systems deserve particular attention, but internal installations should not be overlooked: a server doesn’t need to be publicly accessible to become a useful target after an attacker gains access to an organization’s network.

The ASF has also warned that disabling the feature through the administration interface alone won’t protect older installations:

“Users who cannot upgrade right away should set “enabledForExtensions” to “false” in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the “/roller-services/xmlrpc” servlet mapping, and restart Roller.” concludes the advisory. “Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.”

items.title: Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
items.summary: About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today. My plan today was to write a bit about attacks we are seeing against one of our Java-specific honeypots. But the results can be summarized in one sentence: We are seeing many attacks, but none that exploit Java4Shell (yet). Will it be an important issue? Probably. Should you patch? Sure. Will the world as we know it end? Maybe. So why not go to "Yellow"? This is not a new question. Often people ask why we are on "Green" if they are seeing hundreds or thousands of attacks hitting their system each day. The Internet is a dangerous place. Shouldn't we be on "Yellow" (or "Orange") to reflect that danger? My answer has been: "Green" means the Internet is broken as usual. As long as the status is "Green", you should expect a normal "9-to-5" day. I have heard from organizations that have used our infocon to justify staffing and overtime, and I am well aware of the impact it may have. The reason behind our conservative Infocon is that you can't be alert and "on guard" all the time. An alert status that is "high" all the time is meaningless and counterproductive. You must not treat these recent vulnerabilities as "emergencies". They are the "new normal". Treat them as such. You will not be able to patch nginx2shell across a large organization before the exploit is released. Instead of trying to do the impossible and fail, think beyond the vulnerability of the day. A new reality requires new procedures and techniques. Here are a few ideas: Automate patching as much as possible, in particular for less critical systems. Traditionally, automatic patching had two significant drawbacks. First, you may crash a system because of a failed patch. Secondly, the patch may not be applied correctly, and you treat a vulnerable system as "patched". Select less critical systems that would be at the end of your patch priority list. I'd rather take a system down myself than have ransomware do it for me. Having a system possibly patched is better than being sure the system isn't patched. And of course, there should be some testing, but that can wait a bit longer. This responds well to the faster development of exploits. Reduce your exposure. This should have been a priority years ago. But there are still too many systems connected to the internet that shouldn't be connected. Build a defensible architecture. The same is true for individual applications: reduce the "blast radius" by restricting which data and resources each application can access. And reduce your supply chain exposure. Do you get enough value from tools like Optimizely to justify the risk of them compromising your application? Avoid chasing squirrels. Do not change your plan and drop what you are doing just because the world is going to end. The world may end, in which case, patching one more system is probably not going to make a difference. Whether the world ends or not, at least you will be well-rested to deal with it. During my classes, I am exposed to security professionals from a wide range of backgrounds, working in different industries and countries worldwide. The one thing they all have in common is that they do not have enough time, tools, and sometimes skills to do their job. Making the job you can't do right now any more urgent won't help. Work on tooling and resources, and develop a plan for applying best practices at a sustainable pace. Embrace AI tooling. It is immensely useful for automation. It is even more amazing at helping you get organized. Many partitioners are afraid that AI will do more harm than good, and they are not wrong. But use it where it helps you most. Are you great at writing little scripts but horrible at tracking and inventorying them? Give AI the job you suck at and develop a rapport with your tools. But embracing automation does include embracing AI tooling. Finally, I got a lot of positive feedback on the final "conclusion" of yesterday's podcast, so I am going to link to it directly here: [php2shell] https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33440 [infocon] https://isc.sans.edu/infocon.html -- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter | (c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

items.title: The VPN Gatekeeper's Dilemma: Why VPNs are Always in the Crosshairs
items.summary: The VPN Gatekeeper's DilemmaWhy VPNs are Always in the Crosshairs, what three years of VPN CVEs reveal about enterprise trust, and how ZTNA changes the equation.Every piece of software ships with vulnerabilities, and that includes the security products built to prevent those vulnerabilities from being exploited. The question for any security team is not whether vulnerabilities will surface, but what happens when they do. How much of the environment is exposed, how quickly can an attacker move, and how wide is the blast radius? By these measures, VPN and firewall gateways have a clear structural problem.Since January 2024, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added more than 50 vulnerabilities across VPN and firewall products from major vendors, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. That's roughly one every two to three weeks, and 22 of these have been flagged by CISA as known to have been used in ransomware campaigns. Each came with its own advisory, emergency patch window, and incident-response scramble.Exploited VPN and Firewall flaws from major vendors: Vulnerabilities in VPN and firewall gateway products added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.Taken one at a time, these vulnerabilities look like a string of bad luck for legacy Firewall and VPN providers. Together, they highlight something more fundamental, that traditional VPN architecture puts an enterprise’s trust decisions on the most exposed piece of infrastructure it owns.All of these vendors employ talented engineers who run sophisticated security programs to identify, disclose, and patch vulnerabilities responsibly. When capable teams across an entire product category keep producing the same classes of critical flaws, that’s precisely the point. The problem isn't any single team, it’s the design flaw in the architecture they’re all working with. The Same Failure Modes Keep RepeatingRemoving product and company names makes it abundantly clear that the VPN vulnerabilities attackers actually exploit follow a small number of recurring patterns. Five failure modes account for nearly all of it.CVEAttack VectorWhat the attacker gotCISA KEVCVE-2018-13379SSL VPN path traversal exposing a session filePlaintext VPN credentials; 87,000 devices' credentialsNov 2021CVE-2022-42475Pre-auth heap overflow in SSL VPN daemonRCE; roughly 20,000 FortiGates compromisedDec 2022CVE-2023-4966Memory over-read on GatewayLive session tokens that bypass MFAOct 2023CVE-2023-46805 CVE-2024-21887Auth bypass chained with command injectionPre-auth RCE; CISA ordered federal factory resetsJan 2024CVE-2024-21762Pre-auth out-of-bounds write in SSL VPNRemote code executionFeb 2024CVE-2024-3400Pre-auth command injectionRoot on the firewallApr 2024CVE-2024-24919Arbitrary file read on GatewayCredential and password-hash disclosureMay 2024CVE-2025-0282Pre-auth stack overflowRCE plus malware built to survive upgradesJan 2025CVE-2024-53704SSL VPN authentication bypassHijacked active VPN sessionsFeb 2025CVE-2025-5777Memory over-read on GatewayLive session tokens, againJul 2025CVE-2025-20333 CVE-2025-20362Buffer overflow chained with missing authorizationCode execution; bootkit that survives firmware upgradesSep 2025CVE-2026-24858SSO authentication bypassAdmin access to other customers' devices; zero-dayJan 2026CVE-2026-0257Forgeable authentication override cookieAuthenticated VPN session as any user, no password or MFAMay 2026CVE-2026-0300Pre-auth buffer overflow in Authentication PortalRoot-level remote code executionMay 2026CVE-2026-50751IKEv1 remote access VPN authentication bypassVPN session without a valid passwordJun 20261. Pre-authentication code execution. A VPN concentrator has to accept connections from anyone on the internet before it knows who they are. That listening service parses untrusted input from anonymous senders, which makes it the single most valuable target in the environment. Many of the CVEs listed above are variations of this pattern. A maliciously crafted request reaches code running with high privilege on a device that sits directly between the internet and an enterprise’s internal network.2. Skipped authentication. Attackers obtain or forge the artifact that represents an authenticated session, so the login process never happens. CitrixBleed and CitrixBleed 2 leaked live session tokens from appliance memory. SonicWall vulnerabilities let attackers hijack active SSL VPN sessions. A Check Point exploit granted VPN sessions without a valid password. Palo Alto Networks' CVE-2026-0257 is the most recent example of the pattern, where GlobalProtect offers an "authentication override" option that issues returning users an encrypted cookie so they can skip the login prompt. Rapid7 found that when the certificate used to encrypt those cookies was also the one presented by the portal's HTTPS service, an attacker could pull the public key from the TLS handshake and forge a valid cookie for any user. The result was a fully authenticated VPN session with no username, password, or MFA prompt.3. Credential exposure. Because VPN appliances terminate user authentication, they handle credentials, hashes, and session secrets, and file-read or traversal bugs can turn into credential theft. Fortinet exposed plaintext VPN credentials that eventually led to a public dump covering 87,000 devices. Stolen VPN credentials may also remain valid after the appliance is patched unless every affected password is reset.4. Patch-resistant compromises. Attackers who reach an edge appliances increasingly build persistence into their exploits, so they’re designed to survive a defender's response:In 2024, CISA's Emergency Directive 24-01 required federal agencies to factory-reset compromised Ivanti appliances. A follow-on joint advisory warned that a sophisticated actor might retain root-level persistence even after a reset.In 2025, Fortinet disclosed that attackers had planted a symbolic link on previously compromised FortiGates. The link preserved read-only access to the device's file system even after the original vulnerabilities were patched.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) found that the bootkit used against Cisco ASA devices in 2025 "survives reboots and firmware upgrades." That campaign prompted CISA's Emergency Directive 25-03.Mandiant found Ivanti malware that displayed a fake upgrade progress bar while silently blocking the real one.5. Network-level access. Each of these patterns ends the same way. A VPN's job is to place a remote user on a corporate network. But once an attacker is through the gate, the architecture hands them an internal IP address and routes to everything that address can reach. That's why so many of these CVEs carry CISA's "known ransomware campaign use" flag. The real harm comes from lateral movement that the architecture makes possible. Patching Won’t Close the GapThe standard response to new VPN CVEs is correct: patch software, rotate certificates and credentials, and hunt for indicators of compromise. But the industry data shows that defenders are losing the race.Attackers move in days, where defenders take weeks: Key timing benchmarks (in days), relative to a vendor’s patch release.Exploitation comes first. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 reports that “exploits” were the top initial attack vector for the sixth year in a row. It also found that the mean time to exploit is now negative, which means that on average, vulnerabilities are being exploited before a patch is available.Edge devices are where exploits happen. The 2025 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) found that edge devices and VPNs grew to 22% of vulnerability exploitation targets (from 3%) in a single year. Google's Threat Intelligence Group also counted 21 zero-day exploits in security and networking products in 2025, which was about half of all enterprise-targeted zero-day vulnerabilities it tracked.Vulnerabilities are now the leading way in. The 2026 DBIR found that 31% of breaches now begin with vulnerability exploitation, overtaking credential abuse as the top initial access vector for the first time in the report's 19-year history.Remediation is getting slower. The same report found that only 26% of KEV-listed vulnerabilities were fully resolved, with a median remediation time of 43 days (up from 32 the year before).Organizations see the gap themselves. In the Zscaler ThreatLabz 2026 VPN Risk Report, 54% of organizations said they needed a week or more to patch a critical VPN vulnerability.Forty-three days, or even a week is a relatively long time when exploitation begins in a matter of days (if not sooner). This gap persists even in well-run security programs because the process, and decisions justifying that process is critical:Appliances must be scheduled for maintenance.Remote access can't go down during business hours.High-availability pairs have to be upgraded in sequence.Fixes have to be tested against a configuration that has developed years of exceptions.Government guidance on patching vulnerabilities also reflects this operational reality. The Five Eyes intelligence partners issued a joint series on edge-device security in February 2025. CISA's Binding Operational Directive 26-02 now orders federal agencies to replace edge devices that have reached end of support. In 2024, CISA, the FBI, and international partners jointly urged organizations to move away from traditional VPNs toward zero trust and secure access service edge (SASE) architectures. The Identity Stack Can’t Close the GapOver the past decade, most enterprises have invested heavily in identity-based solutions like single sign-on, multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access, and device posture checks. Those investments help organizations keep unauthorized users out of enterprise networks. In fact, Microsoft's 2025 Digital Defense Report states that MFA can block over 99% of identity-based attacks.When we take a closer look at the failure modes attackers are utilizing, however, it’s clear that identity based solutions have a limited impact. Pre-authentication exploits never reach the identity provider. As far as the appliance is concerned, a forged or stolen session token is presented after authentication has already happened. Leaked credentials can be reused against a gateway that doesn't enforce phishing resistant MFA. In each case the identity stack did its job, but the architecture offered the attacker a path that never touched it.This is the gatekeepers dilemma; a convenient way for legitimate users to access a network is also the most likely attack point, which is why convenience and ingress/egress features keep appearing in these security advisories. Persistent sessions, authentication override cookies, and single sign-on shortcuts exist because VPN reauthentication is painful for users. In a VPN architecture every convenience becomes a trust artifact stored or validated at the internet-facing edge. Administrators are forced to choose between a worse user experience and a larger more vulnerable attack surface.The consequences of that choice are visible in the ransomware data that Zscaler and other organizations have collected over the past decade. The Zscaler ThreatLabz 2026 Ransomware Report found that data exfiltration among the ten most active ransomware groups surged 275.8% year over year, to 896.2 terabytes. It’s Time to Change Where the Architecture SitsZero trust network access (ZTNA) doesn't make software vulnerability-free, and no honest vendor should claim that it does. Every access platform, including its cloud brokers and endpoint clients, is software that needs secure engineering and rapid patching. But ZTNA changes the architecture those vulnerabilities exist in, and that changes everything.Where the trust decision lives: A VPN exposes a gateway and hands out network access. ZTNA exposes nothing and brokers access to one app at a time.Four principles separate these two architectures.Applications are invisible to the internet. In a cloud-native ZTNA model, private applications and the lightweight connectors in front of them make only outbound connections to a cloud exchange. Because nothing listens for inbound connections or exposes public IPs, applications are rendered completely invisible to the internet—leaving no portal for an attacker to discover, fingerprint, scan, or exploit.Access is segmented to specific applications, not the network. Rather than extending subnets or placing users on routed segments, a Zero Trust session connects authorized users, workloads, and AI agents directly to designated applications. By dynamically discovering private workloads and automating least-privilege user-to-app segmentation, lateral threat movement is eliminated. Even if a session is compromised, an attacker never receives an internal IP address or network routes.Trust is continuously verified and reinforced with active containment. Instead of relying on a forgeable bearer token or override cookie cached at an internet-facing gateway, identity, context, and device posture are evaluated continuously in the cloud throughout the session. Users get a seamless experience without perimeter shortcuts—and by integrating deception decoys directly into the access layer, organizations can immediately detect and isolate any post-compromise reconnaissance.Patching moves to the cloud. When the access layer is a multi-tenant cloud service, platform updates are deployed seamlessly without waiting for customer maintenance windows or complex HA upgrades. Modern Zero Trust architectures can also continuously scan private applications for specific exploit paths and apply precise inline virtual patches at machine speed, closing the 43-day remediation gap long before vulnerabilities can be weaponized.Here's how each failure mode plays out under these two models:Failure modeTraditional VPNZero trust architecturePre-auth exploitationConcentrator listens for inbound connections on the public internetApplications and connectors make outbound-only connectionsSession bypassSession state is held and validated at the exposed edgeSessions are brokered per user and per application in the cloud, with continuous identity and posture checksCredential exposureCredentials and session secrets are handled on the applianceAuthentication is delegated to the identity provider; the access layer never stores user credentialsPersistence after patchingCustomer-operated appliance; attacker can hide in firmwareCloud-operated service with no customer-patched gateway to embed malwareNetwork-level accessSuccessful entry places the attacker on the networkUsers only connect to specific applications Solving the Gatekeepers DilemmaCritical vulnerabilities like PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0257), FortiOS (CVE-2024-21762), PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) and others are now endemic, and this trend will likely accelerate due to frontier AI-powered attacks. In addition to data loss and system compromise, CVEs take an enormous toll on organizations in the form of monitoring and patching complex global systems.Statistically, the next critical vulnerability is just a few weeks away. When it arrives, the response playbook will be the all-too-familiar emergency patching, certificate and credential rotation, log reviews, and a lingering concern that the attacker may have left something behind.Organizations can keep running that playbook indefinitely, or they can recognize that the playbook exists because the architecture demands it, and change the architecture.Administrators who enabled the features exploited in recent advisories weren’t being careless, they were trying to solve real user problems within the limits of a legacy architecture. But when dozens of VPN and firewall vulnerabilities have landed on CISA’s KEV catalog in just the last three years, it’s clear that organizations can’t patch their way out of an architectural design flaw. Zero trust solves the gatekeeper’s dilemma by removing exposed gateways altogether, to give users seamless and direct access to applications without exposing your corporate network to the internet.Zscaler Private Access (ZPA), the industry’s first and only AI-powered ZTNA solution, eliminates the gatekeeper’s dilemma by connecting authorized users directly to specific private applications through the Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange. Instead of defending an exposed perimeter gateway that leads to your corporate network, ZPA secures private applications across four core pillars:Hide: Applications are not exposed to the internet. Lightweight App Connectors establish inside-out connections, eliminating public IPs and exposed DMZ gateways so threat actors have nothing to scan, fingerprint, or attack.Segment: Access is brokered on a least-privileged, per-user and per-application basis, with continuous identity and device posture checks. AI-powered app segmentation dynamically recommends and enforces granular user-to-app policies that eliminate lateral movement.Shield: Real-time inline threat and data protection blocks exploits in transit, protecting and patching vulnerable private applications before attackers can strike.Deceive: Native deception and decoys lure, detect, and isolate sophisticated threat actors and malicious insiders attempting post-compromise reconnaissance.Because ZPA is delivered as a cloud-native service across 200+ locations, there is no VPN waiting for an emergency maintenance window when the next critical CVE surfaces.Ready to leave emergency VPN patching behind?Schedule a demo to see Zscaler in actionRead the ThreatLabz 2026 VPN Risk Report

items.title: Hostile Inference: Exploiting Docker Model Runner for Container Escapes
items.summary: Local LLM inference is seeing adoption in default developer workflows, and the tooling that serves those models now ships inside products developers already trust. One of those is Docker Model Runner (DMR), the feature in Docker Desktop that pulls, runs, and serves models locally. In November 2025, we reported ZDI-26-150 / CVE-2026-28400 , a denial-of-service (on macOS) stemming from an unauthenticated argument-injection vulnerability in DMR. A container created with the default set of privileges could overwrite and corrupt the Docker Desktop VM’s data disk. Further analysis, under non-default configurations, turned the same primitive into arbitrary code execution on the host, on both macOS and Windows. In this post, we walk through the full chain: the argument-injection primitive, the host file read/write foothold it grants, how we take partial control of what gets written, and the payoff that turns a constrained file write into arbitrary code execution on the host through Docker Extensions. We then cover two further escapes we found along the way: one from an overly permissive Seatbelt sandbox configuration on macOS, and one that pivots the WSL2 VM-to-host boundary through Docker Extensions. Background: Docker Model Runner and the host boundary Docker Desktop helps run Docker containers on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Docker Desktop for Windows with Windows containers and Docker Desktop for Linux are out of scope for this blog. Since macOS and Windows don’t come with a Linux kernel to run Linux containers, Docker Desktop ships a LinuxKit VM that hosts the container runtime; on macOS the VM runs using the Apple Virtualization Framework , while on Windows it runs under WSL2 by default. Linux containers and the Docker Engine components (runc, containerd, dockerd) run in the Linux VM. Bridging the gap between the host OS and the VM is a daemon called Docker Backend: com.docker.backend (macOS) or com.docker.backend.exe (Windows). This process is responsible for managing the execution environment and brokering all inter-process communication (IPC) across the VM–OS boundary. DMR lets users pull, run, and serve models over OpenAI-compatible APIs using the same idioms as running containers ( docker model pull , docker model run ). Models are distributed as OCI artifacts through OCI-compliant registries and stored on the host. At the time of our research, DMR would create an instance of llama.cpp’s llama-server for inference tasks. DMR is compiled into the Docker Backend. The detail that makes this interesting: on macOS and Windows the inference process does not run inside the VM; it runs on the host, as a child of the Docker Backend, with the privileges of the user running Docker Desktop. Because models are, correctly, treated as untrusted input, the inference process is wrapped in an OS-native sandbox using Seatbelt on macOS and Job Objects on Windows. These are not equivalent boundaries, and that difference carries much of the weight on Windows, as we will see in a bit. The DMR REST API is unauthenticated and reachable from any container at the container-internal DNS name model-runner.docker.internal over HTTP. The question we set out to answer was whether a stock container, created with no additional capabilities, flags, mounts, or privileges, could lead to a container-to-host compromise. The Primitive: Argument Injection in _configure We refer throughout to the DMR repository at docker/model-runner@38a800 . The API is split by two prefixes, both served over model-runner.docker.internal : Backed by the ConfigureRequest struct, the _configure endpoint accepts two JSON properties whose values are appended as command-line arguments for llama-server. It calls the “Configure” method of the scheduler. [1] - The body of the incoming /engines/_configure request is unmarshalled. [2.1 & 2.2] - If the body of the POST request has runtime-flags populated, the value is saved to runtimeFlags as-is. If the body has raw-runtime-flags populated, the value is tokenized through shellwords.Parse(). [3 & 4] - runnerConfig stores the inference server`s backend configuration. [5] - The POST request's model property is used to fetch the model ID for which the config will be modified. [6] - setRunnerConfig persists the modified configuration per model and mode (embedding or non-embedding). At this point, the altered configuration will be applied to the runner's next spawn. Using the chat-completions endpoint /v1/chat/completions , we can load the model that would run the inference server with the altered configuration. Let's see how the arguments propagate. [1] - The backend mode is deduced from the URL path suffix /v1/chat/completions or /v1/completions for completion mode; /v1/embeddings for embedding mode. [2] - The chat completion request's model property contains the model for which chat completion is being invoked. [3] - The scheduler asks the loader using load to execute the request. [4] - If an existing runner for {backend, modelID, mode} is alive, it is reused as-is. Altered configuration is ignored if a runner already exists. [5] - Otherwise, the persisted flags from _configure endpoint are retrieved into runnerConfig . [6] - The runner is created via the package-level run(...) in pkg/scheduling/runner.go, passing the retrieved configuration. [7] - run() calls backend.Run() inside a goroutine, populated with the slot's Unix socket path, the model ID, the request-deduced mode, and the attacker-controlled runnerConfig retrieved from _configure . backend.Run() invokes the inference.Backend interface; the registered and default implementation is llama.cpp`s llama-server. Docker Desktop users received the fixed DMR via version 4.61.0 and later. ZDI-26-451 (Docker Desktop for macOS Inference Server Permissive Allow List Sandbox Escape Vulnerability): • 2026-02-25: Reported to the vendor. • 2026-02-27: Docker merged the tightened Seatbelt profile. • 2026-07-23: Coordinated public release of the advisory. Conclusion Local inference is only going to become more common in developer environments as open-weight models and the hardware to run them improve. The boundaries developers tend to trust (container isolation, sandboxed inference, and marketplace-only extensions) do not automatically extend to the attack paths that arrive with a local-AI stack. A careful audit of deliberate design choices is essential to identify potential vulnerabilities before the most critical components of the supply chain are compromised. You can find me on Twitter at @_niteshsurana , and follow the team on Twitter , Mastodon , LinkedIn , or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

Local LLM inference is seeing adoption in default developer workflows, and the tooling that serves those models now ships inside products developers already trust. One of those is Docker Model Runner (DMR), the feature in Docker Desktop that pulls, runs, and serves models locally. In November 2025, we reported ZDI-26-150 / CVE-2026-28400, a denial-of-service (on macOS) stemming from an unauthenticated argument-injection vulnerability in DMR. A container created with the default set of privileges could overwrite and corrupt the Docker Desktop VM’s data disk. Further analysis, under non-default configurations, turned the same primitive into arbitrary code execution on the host, on both macOS and Windows.

In this post, we walk through the full chain: the argument-injection primitive, the host file read/write foothold it grants, how we take partial control of what gets written, and the payoff that turns a constrained file write into arbitrary code execution on the host through Docker Extensions. We then cover two further escapes we found along the way: one from an overly permissive Seatbelt sandbox configuration on macOS, and one that pivots the WSL2 VM-to-host boundary through Docker Extensions.

Background: Docker Model Runner and the host boundary

Docker Desktop helps run Docker containers on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Docker Desktop for Windows with Windows containers and Docker Desktop for Linux are out of scope for this blog. Since macOS and Windows don’t come with a Linux kernel to run Linux containers, Docker Desktop ships a LinuxKit VM that hosts the container runtime; on macOS the VM runs using the Apple Virtualization Framework, while on Windows it runs under WSL2 by default.

Linux containers and the Docker Engine components (runc, containerd, dockerd) run in the Linux VM. Bridging the gap between the host OS and the VM is a daemon called Docker Backend: com.docker.backend (macOS) or com.docker.backend.exe (Windows). This process is responsible for managing the execution environment and brokering all inter-process communication (IPC) across the VM–OS boundary.

DMR lets users pull, run, and serve models over OpenAI-compatible APIs using the same idioms as running containers (docker model pull, docker model run). Models are distributed as OCI artifacts through OCI-compliant registries and stored on the host. At the time of our research, DMR would create an instance of llama.cpp’s llama-server for inference tasks. DMR is compiled into the Docker Backend. The detail that makes this interesting: on macOS and Windows the inference process does not run inside the VM; it runs on the host, as a child of the Docker Backend, with the privileges of the user running Docker Desktop. Because models are, correctly, treated as untrusted input, the inference process is wrapped in an OS-native sandbox using Seatbelt on macOS and Job Objects on Windows. These are not equivalent boundaries, and that difference carries much of the weight on Windows, as we will see in a bit.

The DMR REST API is unauthenticated and reachable from any container at the container-internal DNS name model-runner.docker.internal over HTTP. The question we set out to answer was whether a stock container, created with no additional capabilities, flags, mounts, or privileges, could lead to a container-to-host compromise.

We refer throughout to the DMR repository at docker/model-runner@38a800. The API is split by two prefixes, both served over model-runner.docker.internal:

Backed by the ConfigureRequest struct, the _configure endpoint accepts two JSON properties whose values are appended as command-line arguments for llama-server. It calls the “Configure” method of the scheduler.

[1] - The body of the incoming /engines/_configure request is unmarshalled.

[2.1 & 2.2] - If the body of the POST request has runtime-flags populated, the value is saved to runtimeFlags as-is. If the body has raw-runtime-flags populated, the value is tokenized through shellwords.Parse().

[3 & 4] - runnerConfig stores the inference server`s backend configuration.

[5] - The POST request's model property is used to fetch the model ID for which the config will be modified.

[6] - setRunnerConfig persists the modified configuration per model and mode (embedding or non-embedding). At this point, the altered configuration will be applied to the runner's next spawn.

[2] - The chat completion request's model property contains the model for which chat completion is being invoked.

[3] - The scheduler asks the loader using load to execute the request.

[4] - If an existing runner for {backend, modelID, mode} is alive, it is reused as-is. Altered configuration is ignored if a runner already exists.

[5] - Otherwise, the persisted flags from _configure endpoint are retrieved into runnerConfig.
