These sinks are a property of llama-server, not the host OS, so the technique carries across platforms unchanged. After this step, we control the destination path (within each platform’s cap), the file name, and, deterministically, a meaningful portion of the content. The remaining question is where a partially-controlled file write becomes arbitrary code execution. The answer is Docker Extensions.

 

The Payoff: Arbitrary Code Execution via Docker Extensions

Docker Extensions let third-party tools plug into Docker Desktop. They consist of a renderer that runs inside Docker Desktop’s Electron UI, an optional container backend, and executables that can be run on the host (as required by the Docker Extension). For a deeper treatment of the extension attack surface, we recommend Orange Cyberdefense’s write-up, “An Offensive Look at Docker Desktop Extensions,” by Leon Jacobs. Docker Desktop’s UI runs Electron with Node.js integration disabled and with context isolation and sandboxing enabled. Extensions have been leveraged before as a route to arbitrary code execution (e.g., CVE-2024-8695, CVE-2024-8696, ZDI-24-1019).

The renderer exposes the Docker Extensions SDK. A ddClient object offers methods for listing containers and images, navigating the Docker Desktop UI, and more. Two are relevant to this chain:

•  ddClient.docker.cli.exec(cmd, [args...]): runs the Docker CLI on the host with arbitrary arguments, including powerful flags such as --privileged, volume mounts, --cap-add, --pid, --ipc, --net, and --device

•  ddClient.extension.host.cli.exec(cmd, [args...]): invokes an executable located in the extension’s dedicated host/ directory on the host, unsandboxed.

Because extensions can trigger privileged host operations by design, their assets (web resources and host executables) are valuable. Furthermore, they are stored on the host at predictable paths. On macOS, those paths sit inside the Seatbelt-permitted Data subtree, which makes them writable via the --log-file primitive. On Windows they live under %APPDATA%\Docker\extensions\, which is why the username leak above matters.

To drop an executable rather than only overwrite a renderer, we also need the host filesystem to be reachable from an additional helper container that is launched by the Extension frontend. By default, Docker Desktop shares host directories into the VM with the privileges of the user running Docker Desktop: on macOS over VirtioFS (/Users, /Volumes, /private, /tmp, /var/folders), and on Windows over WSL2’s 9P protocol, with host drives mounted under /mnt.

In both cases, a container with the VM filesystem bind-mounted can write directly into the Extensions assets directory. This design choice is also why a container that has escaped to the Docker Desktop VM can reach the host filesystem as the current user running Docker Desktop.

Proof of Concept

The PoC has the following prerequisites:

1.    A Docker Extension is installed

2.    The user runs a malicious image or a container gets compromised

3.    The user opens the extension`s UI after running it

Here’s the GGUF Payload:

We create an OCI artifact with a GGUF model with the general.name metadata key's value set to a JS block that invokes two ddClient calls that result in arbitrary code execution on the host. The vm_escape image drops the executable calc.sh on macOS and calc.bat on Windows. The chain runs as follows and is identical on macOS and Windows except for the one Windows-only username-leak step and the platform-specific paths.

1.  Stage 0, from the container: on Windows, first leak the Docker Desktop username, either by pointing a UNC --log-file at an attacker-controlled SMB server or by forcing llama-server to exit on a rejected argument and then reading the username from its error log. In either event, the next step is to use the file-read primitive to read the Docker Desktop logs and enumerate the names of installed extensions; on Windows this read requires the leaked username, while on macOS all logs can be found within the Data subtree.

2.  Stage 1, from the container: pull the crafted GGUF whose general.name is a JS payload that will be rendered in the extension UI. On Windows, use the username from Stage 0 to construct the %APPDATA% extension path. Point --log-file at each installed extension’s index.html and trigger inference. When the chat completion runs, llama-server logs the metadata value, overwriting the extension’s index.html on the host with the inference log containing the JS payload.

3.  Stage 2, from the host: when the user opens the extension, the renderer parses the overwritten index.html and executes the injected JS. It calls ddClient.docker.cli.exec to create a helper container that mounts the VM root at /hostOS and, through the VirtioFS or 9P mount, writes an executable into the extension’s host/ directory (calc.sh on macOS, calc.bat on Windows). It then calls ddClient.extension.host.cli.exec to run the dropped executable on the host, with the Docker Desktop user’s privileges. No sandbox profile gates arbitrary code execution through the extension UI.

Here’s the PoC in action on macOS

And here it is on Windows OS

Going Further: Escaping the macOS Seatbelt Sandbox (ZDI-26-451)

In Stage 2 of the above chain, we use two ddClient calls – one to drop an executable to the host directory, and a second to invoke it. We found that it was possible to achieve arbitrary code execution on the host using a single ddClient call that uses only the Docker CLI.

The llama-server executable is generally run from the user's home directory, as DMR ships an update mechanism that downloads the latest binaries from Docker Hub into ~/.docker/bin/inference/. Our question is: what happens if the binary itself is replaced with an executable script and then invoked through the chat-completions API?

The weakness lies in the Seatbelt profile: com.docker.llama-server’s profile does not deny access to the launchservicesd Mach service. Seatbelt profiles are inherited across standard fork/exec, but macOS offers an alternate execution path through LaunchServices via the /usr/bin/open executable.

When a sandboxed process invokes open, execution is delegated to launchd, and because launchd becomes the parent, the target spawns as a new process, free of the caller’s sandbox restrictions.

Proof of Concept

Simulating a container with access to the Docker Desktop VM via a bind mount (the same VirtioFS sharing described above), we overwrite ~/.docker/bin/inference/com.docker.llama-server with a shell script. The container then calls the chat-completions API, which triggers the Docker Backend to launch our script under the Seatbelt profile.

The script creates an application bundle under /private/var/tmp (a location the profile permits writing to), containing an app that spawns a reverse shell, and then runs open -a /private/var/tmp/poc.app followed by open -a Calculator. Both calls are delegated to LaunchServices and forwarded to launchd, which spawns the apps unsandboxed. The Seatbelt profile is not inherited across that boundary, although the standard macOS protections such as TCC and Gatekeeper still hold.

Going Further: Escaping the WSL2 VM via Docker Extensions (ZDI-26-258)

On Windows, Docker Desktop uses WSL2 as the default backend. For readers interested in WSL2 VM-escape techniques that are structurally independent of DMR, our companion write-up documents several; here we share the first Docker Desktop WSL2 VM-to-host technique we found that pivots on Docker Extensions.

At Pwn2Own Vancouver 2024, STAR Labs researchers demonstrated a Docker Desktop container escape on Ubuntu (ZDI-24-1019 / CVE-2024-6222, fixed in 4.29.0), using an io_uring use-after-free to escape from the container into the VM and Docker Extensions to pivot from the VM to the host.

They installed an arbitrary extension via the extension-manager socket and navigated the UI via a socket named backend.sock to invoke a host binary. In response, Docker disabled io_uring and later enabled a flag in version 4.31.0 to only allow installation of extensions distributed through the Docker Marketplace.

In April 2025 we found that if the Docker Desktop VM is compromised, the “Allow only extensions distributed through the Docker Marketplace” flag could be toggled from the VM itself through the same backend socket. The backend socket is located at /run/host-services/backend.sock in the VM. It exposes an /app/settings API that answers both GET and POST, where GET returns the current settings and POST modifies them.

Flipping onlyMarketPlaceExtensions re-enabled arbitrary extension installation, which in turn leads to arbitrary code execution on the host. We reported our findings as ZDI-26-258 to Docker, to which Docker responded that the attack scenario falls outside of their threat model since the container-to-VM escape prerequisite is privileged in the first place. Hence, if you have a container-to-VM escape for WSL2 or an exposed Docker API (e.g., CVE-2025-9074) or a way to mount Docker sockets, you can use such VM-to-host escapes to achieve arbitrary code execution on the host.

Vendor Response and Patches

For ZDI-26-150, the fix came in three stages.

1. 0699420a (#482, 2025-12-05) removed runtime flags from POST /engines/_configure entirely, replacing them with structured backend-specific configuration.

2. 41dd3f13 (#518, 2025-12-16) reintroduced runtime flags but added validatePathSafety, which rejects any flag or value containing `/` or `\` - fixing the path operations.

3. 9acf1ed9 (#601, 2026-02-09) layered on a strict per-backend allowlist, so only safe flags such as --threads or --ctx-size pass validation.

All three shipped in DMR v1.0.16 with a follow-up hardening commit 78504107 (#667) removing --trust-remote-code, an allowlisted flag that could allow models in vLLM to escape the container. Docker Desktop users received the fixed DMR via version 4.61.0 and later.

For ZDI-26-451, commit 98038869 modified the Seatbelt profile to deny Mach service lookups for com.apple.launchservicesd and com.apple.coreservices.launchservicesd, blocking the LaunchServices path.

Disclosure Timeline

ZDI-26-150 (Docker Desktop for Mac Docker Model Runner Exposed Dangerous Function Denial-of-Service Vulnerability):

•  2025-11-05: Reported to the vendor.

•  2026-03-03: Docker confirmed the fix (CVE-2026-28400, GHSA-m456-c56c-hh5c).

•  2026-03-03: Coordinated public release of the advisory.

ZDI-26-451 (Docker Desktop for macOS Inference Server Permissive Allow List Sandbox Escape Vulnerability):

•  2026-02-25: Reported to the vendor.

•  2026-02-27: Docker merged the tightened Seatbelt profile.

•  2026-07-23: Coordinated public release of the advisory.

Conclusion

Local inference is only going to become more common in developer environments as open-weight models and the hardware to run them improve. The boundaries developers tend to trust (container isolation, sandboxed inference, and marketplace-only extensions) do not automatically extend to the attack paths that arrive with a local-AI stack. A careful audit of deliberate design choices is essential to identify potential vulnerabilities before the most critical components of the supply chain are compromised.

You can find me on Twitter at @_niteshsurana, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

items.title: The Biggest Cyberattacks in Europe (2007–2026): What Happened, How Attackers Got In, and What Followed
items.summary: Europe’s biggest cyberattacks have switched off power in Ukraine, stopped Jaguar Land Rover’s factories for five weeks and exposed data on up to 43 million French jobseekers. We picked 26 attacks from April 2007 to November 2026 that hit organisations in the EU, the wider EEA, the UK, Switzerland or Ukraine. Each one stands out on at least one of four measures: how many people it affected, how long services stayed down, what it cost, or whether it reached a whole country. Every row rests on the victim’s own statements, a regulator, a government, a court or a published forensic report. When only a ransomware gang says something, we call it a claim. For each attack we also checked our GDPR fines tracker for a fine that followed. Six of the 26 led to one. Key findings Four of the five largest data breaches on our list hit France, all since 2024: France Travail (up to 43 million people), Viamedis and Almerys (more than 33 million), Free (24 million subscriber contracts) and Maileva (about 22 million). The fifth is the UK Electoral Commission (about 40 million voters). The costliest is Jaguar Land Rover’s: about £1.9 billion to the UK economy and more than 5,000 organisations affected, by the Cyber Monitoring Centre’s estimate. Only 6 of the 26 attacks led to a GDPR fine, and none of those that stopped hospitals, factories or shops did. The GDPR punishes lost personal data, not downtime. Fines shrink. British Airways’ announced £183.39 million became £20 million; Capita’s provisional £45 million became £14 million. At least 8 of the 26 went through a supplier or hit one, from Ukrainian tax software in 2017 to La Poste’s mail platform in 2026. Missing two-factor login is named in the official reports on British Airways, the British Library, Südwestfalen-IT and the attack on Poland’s energy sector. State attacks moved from websites to utilities. Estonia in 2007 was a flood of traffic; in December 2025 an attack on Poland’s energy sector could have cut power to 500,000 people, the UK government says. It failed.

items.title: Marantz Receivers Now Show Harman’s Privacy Notice With No Way to Say No. The Immigration Line Isn’t the Real Problem
items.summary: Marantz AV receivers are asking their owners to accept a new privacy notice, and the only button on the screen says Acknowledge. The notice belongs to HARMAN, Samsung’s audio subsidiary, which completed its purchase of Marantz’s parent company, Sound United, in September 2025. Since 10 November it lists “immigration” among the kinds of data HARMAN may collect. That line is why a Louis Rossmann video about it has passed 280,000 views since Monday evening. We read the notice, HARMAN’s California supplement and the new Marantz terms. The immigration line comes from HARMAN’s own staff records. The clauses that actually change things for receiver owners are about advertising, Samsung, and what happens if you don’t click. When we published, the story was being discussed on YouTube, the Consumer Rights Wiki and Hacker News. We found no news coverage.

items.title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them
items.summary: New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation OX Security , a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation. OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain. When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical. “The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.” From Breaking Threats to Customer Action To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs. The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected. Through the Response Center, security teams can: Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge. Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence. Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability. Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests. Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity. For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL. Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time. Availability OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website. About OX Security OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments. Contact Head of Communications Jillian Jones OX Security jillian.jones@ox.security

New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation

OX Security, a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation.

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical.

“The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.”

From Breaking Threats to Customer Action

To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs.

The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected.

Through the Response Center, security teams can:

  • Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge.
  • Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence.
  • Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability.
  • Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests.
  • Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity.

For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL.

Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time.

Availability

items.title: Scattered Spider Member Gets Six Years for Phishing and SIM-Swapping Attacks
items.summary: Scottish hacker gets six years for phishing attacks, SIM swapping and stealing $11.6 million in cryptocurrency from US victims. Tyler Robert Buchanan (24) of Dundee, Scotland, was sentenced to 72 months in federal prison. The Justice Department says he conspired to hack at least a dozen companies through text message phishing and stole over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individuals across the US. He pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, and he’s the fifth and final defendant sentenced in this case. Employees who typed their credentials into those pages handed over account access, personal information and company data. The conspirators built a phishing kit that captured those logins and piped them straight to a Telegram channel Buchanan ran with another member. When police searched his home in Scotland in April 2023, they found files tied to numerous victim companies. Spanish police arrested the British national who was suspected of being a key member of the cybercrime group Scattered Spider (also known as UNC3944 , 0ktapus ). The man was arrested in Palma de Mallorca while attempting to fly to Italy. During the arrest, police confiscated a laptop and a mobile phone. The arrest resulted from a joint operation conducted by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Spanish Police. Spanish police tracked the suspect to Mallorca after he entered Spain via Barcelona in late May 2024. Buchanan has been in U.S. custody since April 2025. Between 2021 and 2023, he and his group targeted companies and individuals across several sectors. They sent large SMS phishing campaigns that mimicked trusted services and tricked employees into sharing credentials and personal data. Using this access, they broke into corporate systems and stole sensitive information, including intellectual property and user data. “The SMS phishing messages contained links to phishing websites designed to look like legitimate websites of a victim company or a contracted IT or BPO supplier. The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), account usernames, and passwords.” reads the press release published by DoJ. “As part of the scheme, the conspirators created a phishing kit that captured login credentials entered the fraudulent phishing websites by a victim company’s employees. The stolen credentials were then transmitted to an online Telegram channel administered by Buchanan and another co-conspirator.” Buchanan admitted he kept files linked to many victim companies at his home in Scotland. He and his accomplices used stolen data from corporate breaches to target individuals and access their cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing millions. To do this, they broke into online accounts and carried out SIM swap attacks, taking control of victims’ phone numbers and intercepting two-factor authentication codes sent via SMS or calls. This let them bypass security protections and fully access accounts. Investigators also found sensitive data on his devices, including names, addresses, login credentials, and even cryptocurrency seed phrases tied to victims’ wallets, showing how the group combined corporate intrusions and personal targeting to maximize profits. “Buchanan further admitted that he and several co-conspirators used the information stolen from company intrusions to identify and gain access to virtual currency accounts and wallets belonging to individual victims to steal millions of dollars’ worth of virtual currency.” continues press release. Noah Michael Urban , also known as “Sosa” and “Elijah,” received a 10-year prison sentence and must pay $13 million in restitution after pleading guilty to fraud charges. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo each got 45 months, and Joel Martin Evans got two years. The cybercrime group Scattered Spider is suspected of hacking into hundreds of organizations over the past two years, including Twilio , LastPass , DoorDash , and Mailchimp . Scattered Spider members are part of a broader cybercriminal community called “ The Com ,” where hackers brag about high-profile cyber thefts, typically initiated through social engineering tactics like phone, email, or SMS scams to gain access to corporate networks. “Those thefts had severe, life-altering consequences for many victims and underscore both the seriousness and far-reaching impact of this conspiracy,” prosecutors argued in a sentencing memorandum. A restitution hearing is set for 11 December. The investigation pulled in the FBI, the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, Police Scotland, Spain’s Cuerpo Nacional de Policía, and FBI field offices in four cities. SIM swapping defeats SMS-based two-factor authentication specifically, so an authenticator app or a hardware key closes that door even when a text message doesn’t look suspicious. The case is a reminder that your phone number is a password too, and one you can’t change as easily. The Justice Department sums up the method plainly: “SIM swapping” is a technique in which a criminal fraudulently induces a mobile carrier to reassign a cell phone number from the legitimate subscriber’s SIM card to a SIM card controlled by another without the legitimate subscriber’s authorization or knowledge. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Scattered Spider)

items.title: HIPAA Privacy Rule
items.summary: The HIPAA Privacy Rule provides a federal floor of privacy standards that protects individuals’ health information and other identifying information by limiting the permissible uses and disclosure of such information by “covered entities” and “business associates” without authorization. The HIPAA Privacy Rule also gives individuals the rights to control how their health information is used and disclosed, to request copies of information maintained about them, and request corrections when omissions or errors exist. This guide to the HIPAA Privacy Rule explains why it exists, who it applies to, what it protects, and how to maintain compliance. It should be used in conjunction with our free, easy to use HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist PDF which can be ordered by using any form on this page. What is the Privacy Rule in the Context of HIPAA? In the context of HIPAA , the Privacy Rule is a subpart of the Administrative Simplifications Regulations (45 CFR Parts 160,162, and 164). The protections provided by the Privacy Rule to individually identifiable health information apply to other subparts of the Administrative Simplification Regulations and how the standards within those subparts are applied. For this reason, it is important for entities that are not usually required to comply with the HIPAA Privacy Rule (i.e., data storage services and vendors of personal health devices) to understand what the Rule protects and how. It can also be useful for those whose information is protected by the Privacy Rule to understand how the HIPAA privacy standards are applied to prevent misconceptions. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Get The HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist Free and Immediate Download Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form. Business Email * Name * First Last Number * Company Name * Download Free Checklist Delivered via email so please ensure you enter your email address correctly. Your Privacy Respected HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy HIPAA Privacy Rule Fact Sheet The Privacy Rule was published in 2002. It is one of several sets of standards that evolved from HIPAA. It stipulates permissible uses and disclosures of Protected Health Information and individuals’ rights. Most health plans, health care clearinghouses, and healthcare providers are required to comply with the Privacy Rule. Business Associates may also be required to comply with the Privacy Rule depending on the service being provided. The Privacy Rule defines Protected Health Information to include identifiers maintained in the same designated record set. All patients and plan members must be given a HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices on the first encounter or as soon as reasonable. The Notice of Privacy Practices must explain what Protected Health Information may be disclosed, to whom, and why. The Notice of Privacy Practices must also explain an individual’s right to access, amend, or transfer their Protected Health Information. If organizations violate the HIPAA Rules, individuals have the right to complain to the organization or HHS’ Office for Civil Rights. The Office for Civil Rights has the authority to impose corrective action plans or financial penalties on noncompliant organizations. Who Falls Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule Before discussing what information is protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule and how the HIPAA Privacy Standards ensure individuals’ rights, it is important to understand who the HIPAA Rules apply to because some organizations are not required to comply with every HIPAA Rule or every part of every HIPAA Rule. It is also the case that exceptions can exist to the applicability of each Rule. Most health plans, health care clearinghouses, and healthcare providers that conduct electronic transactions listed in Part 162 of the Administrative Requirements are required to comply with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the HIPAA Security Rule, and the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule that was introduced as part of the HITECH Act in 2009. Collectively, these organizations are referred to as “covered entities”. Business associates are also required to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule and HIPAA Breach Notification Rule; and, depending on the nature of the service provided for or on behalf of a covered entity, any applicable standards of the Administrative Requirements and HIPAA Privacy Rule. Some of the exceptions mentioned above include: Health care providers that bill clients directly are not covered entities. Neither are insurance issuers who offer health insurance as a secondary benefit. Neither are health plans for certain types of benefits that are offered separately. The HIPAA Rules may apply to employers who self-administer a group health plan. But not to employment records containing individually identifiable health information. Vendors of personal health devices are only required to comply with HIPAA when they provide a service as a business associate. To further complicate who the HIPAA Rules apply to, some organizations can be hybrid entities when some of their activities are covered by HIPAA, while others are not; or temporarily subject to the HIPAA Rules, for example, when a healthcare provider who does not qualify as a covered entity provides a service for or on behalf of a covered entity as a business associate. In such cases, the healthcare provider has to comply with the HIPAA Rules for as long as they are providing the service. Why Does the HIPAA Privacy Rule Exist? Prior to the passage of HIPAA, the privacy of medical records was determined by a patchwork of state regulations. The first Clinton administration (1993 to 1997) attempted to introduce a comprehensive federal health privacy framework, but the ambitious Health Security Act failed due to opposition from the private insurance industry and a lack of congressional support. After the Act failed, Congress attempted to pass separate medical privacy legislation but could not agree on a national standard. Consequently, the buck was passed to the Secretary of Health and Human Services, who was instructed in the text of HIPAA to make recommendations “with respect to the privacy of certain health information”. At a minimum, the recommendations had to include: The rights that an individual who is a subject of individually identifiable health information should have. The procedures that should be established for the exercise of such rights. The uses and disclosures of such information that should be authorized or required. The instruction adds that, if Congress does not pass legislation to protect the privacy of individually identifiable health information within three years of the passage of HIPAA, the Secretary shall promulgate a further Rule addressing the minimum recommendations. Congress did not pass privacy legislation within three years and a proposed HIPAA Privacy Rule was published in 1999. After years of addressing stakeholders’ comments, the HIPAA Final Privacy Rule was published in 2002 and became effective in 2003. Business Email * Name * First Last Number * Company Name * Download Free Checklist Delivered via email so please ensure you enter your email address correctly. Your Privacy Respected HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy What Information is Protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule? Any individually identifiable health information relating to an individual’s past, present, or future physical or mental condition, treatment for the condition, or payment for the treatment is protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule, along with individually identifiable non-health information maintained in the same “designated record set”. Information maintained in a designated record set is known as Protected Health Information (PHI) , even though elements of the set may not contain health information. This definition of what information is protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule can cause confusion because some sources claim that all information relating to an individual is protected – and that is not always the case. Individually identifiable health information and any other information that identifies – or that could be used to identify – the subject of the health information (known as an “identifier”) is protected only while it is maintained in a designated record set. Whenever identifiers are maintained separately from individually identifiable health information, they are no longer Protected Health Information and the protections of the HIPAA Privacy Rule no longer apply. As an example, if a designated record set includes a patient’s diagnosis, their home telephone number, the name of their partner, and their healthcare payment details, all four elements of information are protected while they are maintained in the same designated record set. If a separate record set is created containing a copy of the home telephone number and partner’s name (perhaps to provide the partner with an update on the patient’s health), these elements are not protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule because there is no health information included in the record set. It is important to be aware that in such circumstances, although the HIPAA Rules do not apply, state privacy and security rules may. How is Information Protected by the HIPAA Privacy Regulations? The HIPAA Privacy Regulations, or “standards”, protect information by stipulating when uses and disclosures or Protected Health Information are required, permitted, or subject to an individual’s authorization. There are only two occasions when uses and disclosures are required; when an individual exercises their access rights and when access is required by HHS’ Office for Civil Rights for an investigation or compliance review. Both of these events are discussed in greater detail later. Permissible uses and disclosures include those necessary to carry out treatment, payment, or health care operations, those required by law or for public health activities, and those necessary to avert a serious threat to health or safety. Among the disclosures permitted by HIPAA, there are some that are required by state laws. For example, disclosures to report abuse, neglect, or domestic abuse. Some “permissible” disclosures may also be “required” during emergency incidents. Other than the uses and disclosures required or permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Regulations, and some for which the individual should be given an opportunity to object when feasible, all other uses and disclosures of Protected Health Information are prohibited unless they are authorized by the individual who is the subject of the Protected Health Information or their personal representative. Such uses and disclosures include uses for marketing and disclosures of psychotherapy notes. Authorizations have to be written in clear language and explain to the individual what Protected Health Information is being used or disclosed, who to, and what for. If the covered entity is receiving a remuneration for the use or disclosure, this has to be included in the authorization, as does a warning that the covered entity may have no control over further disclosures of the Protected Health Information if, for example, it is published on a social media platform . Get The HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist Free and Immediate Download Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form. Business Email * Name * First Last Number * Company Name * Download Free Checklist Delivered via email so please ensure you enter your email address correctly. Your Privacy Respected HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy How do the HIPAA Privacy Standards Ensure Individuals’ Rights? The HIPAA Privacy Standards ensure individuals’ rights by first requiring covered health plans and healthcare providers to give a HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices to new patients or plan members on the “first encounter” whenever possible or as soon as reasonable afterwards. The Notice must describe the ways in which the covered entity may use or disclose Protected Health Information and describe how individuals can exercise their rights to access copies of their Protected Health Information. The right to access copies of Protected Health Information is the “required” disclosure mentioned above, but it is important for individuals to understand they are only able to access information maintained in a designated record set. It is also important to understand that complying with an access request may take some time when multiple designated record sets are maintained per individual, or when Protected Health Information is in the possession of a business associate. Once an individual has received a copy of their Protected Health Information the HIPAA Privacy Standards allows individuals to request corrections to the information if it is inaccurate or incomplete. Individuals can also request information is transferred to another provider, or that specific information is withheld from certain organizations. For example, if a patient has paid for treatment privately, they have the right to request this information is withheld from their insurer. Individuals also have the right to request an accounting of disclosures. This document should contain a list of the times when Protected Health Information has been disclosed for reasons other than those permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Regulations or authorized by the individual themselves. Individuals have the right to query any entry on the accounting of disclosures and, if not satisfied with the response, make a complaint about their privacy rights being violated. Who Enforces HIPAA Privacy Rules? The Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights (OCR) is the enforcer of the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Noncompliance could lead to civil and criminal penalties, highlighting the importance of rigorous adherence. What Happens if You Violate HIPAA Privacy Regulations? The violation of privacy rights is one of the leading reasons for complaints to HHS’ Office for Civil Rights; and when a complaint is received by the agency, it has to be reviewed and investigated if it appears there has been a violation of HIPAA regulations. When HHS’ Office for Civil Rights conducts an investigation, a covered entity must disclose whatever Protected Health Information is necessary for the agency to conclude its investigation – as mentioned previously in the section explaining how information is protected. Most violations of HIPAA regulations are resolved by technical assistance or a corrective action plan. This means that the covered entity or business associate may have to develop and implement new policies and procedures to resolve the issue responsible for the violation of the HIPAA regulations. The organization may then have to train its workforce on the new policies and procedures and, depending on the scale of the violation(s), undergo a period of compliance monitoring. In cases where there has been a willful neglect of the HIPAA regulations, HHS’ Office for Civil Rights has the authority to impose civil monetary penalties on noncompliant organizations. Historically, financial settlements and civil monetary penalties have been reserved for the worst offenders following large-scale data breaches. More recently, the agency has pursued a campaign to address violations of the HIPAA regulations that deny individuals their Privacy Rule rights. Get The HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist Free and Immediate Download Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form. Business Email * Name * First Last Number * Company Name * Download Free Checklist Delivered via email so please ensure you enter your email address correctly. Your Privacy Respected HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy As well as organizations being penalized for non-compliance, members of the workforce can be sanctioned as well. The degree of sanction will depend on the nature of the violation and the content of the organization’s sanctions policy. In the worst cases of knowing and wrongful disclosures of PHI for personal gain, cases can be referred to the Department of Justice – who can pursue custodial sentences of up to ten years and fines of up to $250,000. When was the Last Update to the HIPAA Privacy Rule? The most recent update to the HIPAA Privacy Rule is the final rule HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens . The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) announced it on November 16, 2026, and it was published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. The update was a long time coming. HHS first proposed the changes in December 2020, and the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking was published in the Federal Register on January 21, 2021, almost six years before the final rule was issued. What were the Major Changes Introduced by the Update? The 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule update has three main aims: strengthening the individual right of access, making it easier to share information for care coordination, and reducing the administrative burden on covered entities. The final rule also adds definitions of “electronic health record” and “personal health application” to the Privacy Rule. Changes to Patients’ Right of Access The biggest change for most covered entities is the time allowed to respond to access requests. It has been cut from 30 days to 15 days. The option of one 30-day extension remains. Individuals can ask for copies of ePHI in a designated record set to be sent to a personal health application of their choice. Covered entities only have to do this if the ePHI is readily producible in that form. They don’t have to implement new technology to make it possible, but they must use technology they already have or that other laws require. Individuals can also direct a covered health care provider to send ePHI held in an electronic health record to a third party. Covered entities can no longer charge individuals for inspecting their PHI in person or for accessing their ePHI through an internet-based method, such as a patient portal or a personal health app connected through an API. Access that involves workforce labor, such as emailing a PDF on request, is not considered internet-based, so a reasonable, cost-based fee may still be charged. For other types of access, fees are limited to: labor for copying supplies for non-electronic copies postage preparing a summary or explanation, if the individual agrees to it Covered entities with a website must post a fee schedule on it and make the schedule available at the point of service. They are also encouraged to consider the financial circumstances of the person making the request. Covered entities must not impose unreasonable identity verification requirements. They also must not create barriers to access, such as accepting requests only through a patient portal. Changes to Facilitate Better Care Coordination The final rule expressly allows covered entities to disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management to third parties, such as social services agencies, community-based organizations, and home and community-based services providers. The minimum necessary standard still applies to these disclosures where relevant. A covered entity is not liable if the recipient later misuses or improperly discloses the information. The definition of health care operations has also been clarified to include care coordination and case management at both the individual and population level. This is particularly relevant to health plans. Reducing the Administrative Burden Covered health care providers no longer have to make a good faith effort to obtain written acknowledgment that a patient received the Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP). They also no longer have to document why an acknowledgment was not obtained. HHS estimates that this change alone will save around $798 million a year. Related changes to reduce the administrative burden include: Disclosures to Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) communications assistants are permitted, and TRS providers are no longer considered business associates. The permission to use and disclose the PHI of Armed Forces personnel for mission readiness now covers all uniformed services, including the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps and the NOAA Commissioned Corps. Other Changes Introduced by the Update Other changes introduced by the 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule update include that individuals have the right to discuss the content of the Notice of Privacy Practices (NPPs) with a designated contact, and NPPs must be updated to explain this new right. The NPP header must also refer to “health information” rather than “medical information.” The right to receive an NPP is also extended to inmates of correctional facilities that qualify as HIPAA covered entities. Several proposals from the 2021 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking were not finalized. These include allowing individuals to take photographs of their PHI during in-person inspections, changing the standard for disclosures to family members and caregivers from “professional judgment” to “good faith,” and capping the fees that can be charged for sending copies of PHI to third parties. How Long do HIPAA-Regulated Entities Have to Comply with the 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule Update? The final rule takes effect on January 18, 2027, 60 days after it was published in the Federal Register. Covered entities and business associates then have a further 180 days to comply. The compliance date is July 17, 2027. After that date, OCR can enforce the new requirements and may impose civil monetary penalties for noncompliance. Until then, the current requirements still apply, including the 30-day timeframe for responding to access requests. By the compliance date, covered entities need to update their policies and procedures, publish their access fee schedules, and retrain their workforces on the new requirements. They also need to have their revised NPPs available on their websites, posted at their facilities, and ready to give to new patients. There is a longer transition period for business associate agreements. Existing agreements that comply with the current requirements will be deemed compliant until whichever of these comes first: the agreement is renewed or modified after July 17, 2027 January 18, 2028 The same transition period applies to agreements between business associates and their subcontractors. Verbal arrangements are not covered by the transition provision. HIPAA Privacy Rule Compliance Overview To support HIPAA compliance efforts, the information in this article should be used in conjunction with our free, easy to use HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist PDF which can be ordered by using any form on this page. Privacy Rule HIPAA compliance necessitates organizational actions and technical precautions. Organizationally, covered entities and business associates must implement and enforce privacy policies and procedures in line with the HIPAA Privacy Rule. A privacy official should be appointed to oversee the development and implementation of these policies. Regular training sessions must be held to familiarize workforce members with these guidelines. Covered entities must also inform individuals about their privacy rights and the potential use of their information. A HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices should be readily available for anyone requesting it. Breaches of unsecured PHI must be reported to the individuals affected, the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and in certain circumstances, to the media. For instances where PHI needs to be shared, covered entities should create contracts ensuring that business associates will protect the information. These contracts, known as Business Associate Agreements (BAAs), are a critical part of Privacy Rule HIPAA compliance. HIPAA Privacy Rule FAQs What are the eighteen identifiers that determine whether health information should be protected? There is sometimes a misconception that the eighteen “HIPAA identifiers” listed under §164.514 of the HIPAA Privacy Rule are Protected Health Information at all times. This is not the case. These identifiers relate to the information that must be removed from a designated record set before any remaining health or payment information is considered de-identified under the safe harbor method. As explained above, any identifier that is maintained in a designated record set along with health or payment information is protected while it is maintained in the same designated record set. When maintained in a database that does not contain health or payment information, identifiers are not protected by HIPAA, although state privacy and security laws may apply. It is important to be aware that the list of eighteen HIPAA identifiers was compiled more than twenty years ago and has not been updated to reflect changes in how individuals can be identified. For example, if details of a patient’s emotional support animal are maintained in a designated record set, and the patient could be identified by the emotional support animal, these details also need to be removed from a designated record set before any remaining health information is de-identified. Your Privacy Respected HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy What is the difference between health information, individually identifiable health information, and Protected Health Information? In the context of the HIPAA Privacy Rule, health (or payment) information does not include any information about who a health condition, treatment for the condition, or payment for the treatment relates to. “The patient has a broken leg” or “the patient’s treatment is being paid by Medicare” is health information for the purposes of complying with the HIPAA Privacy Rule. As soon as any element of information is combined with health or payment information that could identify or be used to identify an individual, it becomes individually identifiable health information. If the identifying information is maintained by a covered entity or business associate in the same designated record set as the health information, it is Protected Health Information. Within HIPAA, how does security differ from privacy? The HIPAA Privacy Rule and the HIPAA Security Rule both have the same objectives with regards to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of Protected Health Information. The difference between them is that the HIPAA Security Rule only applies to electronic Protected Health Information, while the HIPAA Privacy Rule applies to Protected Health Information in any format. Who enforces the HIPAA Privacy Rule? Externally, the HIPAA Privacy Rule is enforced by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights (OCR). OCR officers are most often made aware of HIPAA Privacy Rule violations via public complaints, HIPAA audits, and covered entities complying with the requirements to notify OCR of data breaches. OCR also enforces the HIPAA Security Rule and HIPAA Breach Notification Rule. Internally, the HIPAA Privacy Rule is enforced by a Privacy Officer. The Privacy Officer has the responsibility of conducting risk assessments, developing policies and procedures to reduce risks to a reasonable level, training members of the workforce on the policies and procedures, and enforcing the HIPAA sanctions policy for violations of the organization’s policies and procedures. Are there specific technologies that are HIPAA compliant? No technology is HIPAA-compliant because it is how the technology is configured and used that determines compliance, not the capabilities of the technology itself. If a technology is implemented that has access to Protected Health Information, a Business Associate Agreement may have to be in place with the vendor for the technology to be considered capable of supporting HIPAA compliance. What is the Minimum Necessary Standard? The Minimum Necessary standard stipulates that uses and disclosures of Protected Health Information must be limited to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the use or disclosure. The standard applies to most uses and disclosures, but there are exceptions to this standard it is important to be aware of in order to avoid unnecessary complaints. Your Privacy Respected HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy In what circumstances can an individual object to disclosures of Protected Health Information? These most often relate to disclosing information via a facility directory or notifying an individual’s family when (for example) an individual is admitted to hospital. Individuals can consent to limited information being disclosed in these circumstances or, if the individual is incapable of providing consent, covered entities can determine whether the disclosure is in the best interests of the individual. The information that can be disclosed in such circumstances is listed in §164.510 . What is the difference between individual consent and individual authorization? For any other uses or disclosures of Protected Health Information other than those required or permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Rule, an individual has to give their consent or authorization. Consent, which can be verbal, is only allowed for the uses and disclosures included in §164.510. All other uses and disclosures require a written authorization signed by the individual. As a guideline, consent relates to obtaining permission for routine activities. Authorization is necessary when PHI is going to be used or disclosed for a non-routine activity. What happens if you disclose Protected Health Information without an authorization? If you disclose Protected Health Information impermissibly, it is a violation of HIPAA. The consequences of any HIPAA violation depend on various factors such as the nature of the violation, the harm to the individual, the organization’s sanctions policy, and the previous compliance history of both the person responsible for the violation and the organization they work for. The impermissible disclosure of Protected Health Information may qualify as a data breach, in which case both the individual and HHS’ Office of Civil Rights need to be notified of the event. If the disclosure does not qualify as a data breach, the individual can still complain to HHS’ Office for Civil Rights, who may decide to investigate the organization depending on its compliance history. What are the 3 Rules of HIPAA? The three Rules of HIPAA that covered entities are required to comply with are the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the HIPAA Security Rule, and the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule which was introduced via the HITECH Act of 2009. There are two other Rules commonly associated with HIPAA; the HIPAA Enforcement Rule, which describes the process for compliance investigations, and the Omnibus HIPAA Final Rule which, in 2013, updated the HIPAA Privacy Rule and HIPAA Security Rule with other measures introduced by the HITECH Act. In addition, it is important not to overlook the HIPAA General Provisions (Part 160, Subpart A) which explains many of the terms used in the HIPAA laws and regulations, and the Organization Requirements of Part 164 (§164.105) which explain which components of the HIPAA Privacy Rule apply to non-standard covered entities (i.e., Organized Health Care Arrangements, etc.). Covered entities and business associates are also required to comply with, or oversee compliance with, the Part 162 Rules relating to transactions and code sets. What is the purpose of the Privacy Rule? The purpose of the Privacy Rule is to set a federal floor of privacy protections for individuals’ individually identifiable health information. The Privacy Rule also gives individuals an opportunity to better control how their health information is used and disclosed, to take a more active role in their healthcare, and choose the best healthcare provider for their requirements. Who is not covered by the HIPAA Privacy Rule? Any organization that does not qualify as a covered entity or that does not provide a service for or on behalf of a covered entity as a business associate is not covered by the HIPAA Privacy Rule. It is important to be aware that business associates are only required to comply with the Privacy Rule “where provided”, and this is usually established in a Business Associate Agreement. Some business associates may not be covered by the HIPAA Privacy Rule depending on the service provided, and may only required to comply with the HIPAA Security and Breach Notification Rules. When does the Privacy Rule not apply to health information? The Privacy Rule does not apply to health information in a number of circumstances. These include when an organization does not qualify as a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, when the health information belongs to a student and is covered by FERPA, when other, more stringent, Rules than HIPAA apply, and when an individual has authorized a use or disclosure which may be subject to further uses and disclosures that a covered entity has no control over (i.e., when it is published on social media). Why is the Privacy Rule important? Research suggests when patients believe their health information is protected, they are more willing to discuss intimate details with healthcare providers. With more information, healthcare providers can make more accurate diagnoses and prescribe more effective courses of treatment, leading to better patient outcomes, higher morale in the workplace, and increased hospital satisfaction scores. What are HIPAA Rules and why are they different? The HIPAA Rules are the standards within the Administrative Simplification Regulations that govern how covered entities must protect the privacy of Protected Health Information, how electronic Protected Health Information should be safeguarded to ensure its confidentiality, integrity, and availability, and how covered entities should respond in the event of an impermissible use or disclosure or a data breach. The reason they may be considered “different” is that they are a baseline of privacy and security standards. In many states, more stringent privacy and/or security standards, or regulations providing individuals with greater access rights, overlay parts of HIPAA. Some states also have privacy and security standards that cross borders, protecting the individually identifiable health information of state residents wherever they are in the United States. What is the difference between the Privacy Rule of HIPAA, the HIPAA Privacy Law, and the HIPAA Privacy Act? There is no difference between the Privacy Rule of HIPAA, the HIPAA Privacy Law, and the HIPAA Privacy Act. These are names sometimes used to describe the “Standards for the Privacy of Individual Identifiable Health Information” published in Subpart E of Part 164 of the HIPAA Administrative Simplification Regulations. Most sources, including the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights, refer to the Standards as the “HIPAA Privacy Rule” to avoid confusing the agency-promulgated standards with Laws or Acts passed by Congress. For example, the HIPAA Act was passed by Congress, but the HIPAA Rules were promulgated by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The HIPAA Privacy Rule provides a federal floor of privacy standards that protects individuals’ health information and other identifying information by limiting the permissible uses and disclosure of such information by “covered entities” and “business associates” without authorization. The HIPAA Privacy Rule also gives individuals the rights to control how their health information is used and disclosed, to request copies of information maintained about them, and request corrections when omissions or errors exist.

This guide to the HIPAA Privacy Rule explains why it exists, who it applies to, what it protects, and how to maintain compliance. It should be used in conjunction with our free, easy to use HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist PDF which can be ordered by using any form on this page.

What is the Privacy Rule in the Context of HIPAA?

In the context of HIPAA, the Privacy Rule is a subpart of the Administrative Simplifications Regulations (45 CFR Parts 160,162, and 164). The protections provided by the Privacy Rule to individually identifiable health information apply to other subparts of the Administrative Simplification Regulations and how the standards within those subparts are applied.

For this reason, it is important for entities that are not usually required to comply with the HIPAA Privacy Rule (i.e., data storage services and vendors of personal health devices) to understand what the Rule protects and how. It can also be useful for those whose information is protected by the Privacy Rule to understand how the HIPAA privacy standards are applied to prevent misconceptions.

HIPAA Journal Privacy Policy

HIPAA Privacy Rule Fact Sheet
  • The Privacy Rule was published in 2002. It is one of several sets of standards that evolved from HIPAA.
  • It stipulates permissible uses and disclosures of Protected Health Information and individuals’ rights.
  • Most health plans, health care clearinghouses, and healthcare providers are required to comply with the Privacy Rule.
  • Business Associates may also be required to comply with the Privacy Rule depending on the service being provided.
  • The Privacy Rule defines Protected Health Information to include identifiers maintained in the same designated record set.
  • All patients and plan members must be given a HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices on the first encounter or as soon as reasonable.
  • The Notice of Privacy Practices must explain what Protected Health Information may be disclosed, to whom, and why.
  • The Notice of Privacy Practices must also explain an individual’s right to access, amend, or transfer their Protected Health Information.
  • If organizations violate the HIPAA Rules, individuals have the right to complain to the organization or HHS’ Office for Civil Rights.
  • The Office for Civil Rights has the authority to impose corrective action plans or financial penalties on noncompliant organizations.
Who Falls Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule

Before discussing what information is protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule and how the HIPAA Privacy Standards ensure individuals’ rights, it is important to understand who the HIPAA Rules apply to because some organizations are not required to comply with every HIPAA Rule or every part of every HIPAA Rule. It is also the case that exceptions can exist to the applicability of each Rule.

Most health plans, health care clearinghouses, and healthcare providers that conduct electronic transactions listed in Part 162 of the Administrative Requirements are required to comply with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the HIPAA Security Rule, and the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule that was introduced as part of the HITECH Act in 2009. Collectively, these organizations are referred to as “covered entities”.

Business associates are also required to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule and HIPAA Breach Notification Rule; and, depending on the nature of the service provided for or on behalf of a covered entity, any applicable standards of the Administrative Requirements and HIPAA Privacy Rule. Some of the exceptions mentioned above include:

  • Health care providers that bill clients directly are not covered entities.
  • Neither are insurance issuers who offer health insurance as a secondary benefit.
  • Neither are health plans for certain types of benefits that are offered separately.
  • The HIPAA Rules may apply to employers who self-administer a group health plan.
  • But not to employment records containing individually identifiable health information.
  • Vendors of personal health devices are only required to comply with HIPAA when they provide a service as a business associate.

To further complicate who the HIPAA Rules apply to, some organizations can be hybrid entities when some of their activities are covered by HIPAA, while others are not; or temporarily subject to the HIPAA Rules, for example, when a healthcare provider who does not qualify as a covered entity provides a service for or on behalf of a covered entity as a business associate. In such cases, the healthcare provider has to comply with the HIPAA Rules for as long as they are providing the service.

Why Does the HIPAA Privacy Rule Exist?

Prior to the passage of HIPAA, the privacy of medical records was determined by a patchwork of state regulations. The first Clinton administration (1993 to 1997) attempted to introduce a comprehensive federal health privacy framework, but the ambitious Health Security Act failed due to opposition from the private insurance industry and a lack of congressional support.

After the Act failed, Congress attempted to pass separate medical privacy legislation but could not agree on a national standard. Consequently, the buck was passed to the Secretary of Health and Human Services, who was instructed in the text of HIPAA to make recommendations “with respect to the privacy of certain health information”. At a minimum, the recommendations had to include:

  • The rights that an individual who is a subject of individually identifiable health information should have.
  • The procedures that should be established for the exercise of such rights.
  • The uses and disclosures of such information that should be authorized or required.

The instruction adds that, if Congress does not pass legislation to protect the privacy of individually identifiable health information within three years of the passage of HIPAA, the Secretary shall promulgate a further Rule addressing the minimum recommendations. Congress did not pass privacy legislation within three years and a proposed HIPAA Privacy Rule was published in 1999. After years of addressing stakeholders’ comments, the HIPAA Final Privacy Rule was published in 2002 and became effective in 2003.

What Information is Protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule?

Any individually identifiable health information relating to an individual’s past, present, or future physical or mental condition, treatment for the condition, or payment for the treatment is protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule, along with individually identifiable non-health information maintained in the same “designated record set”.

Information maintained in a designated record set is known as Protected Health Information (PHI), even though elements of the set may not contain health information.

This definition of what information is protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule can cause confusion because some sources claim that all information relating to an individual is protected – and that is not always the case. Individually identifiable health information and any other information that identifies – or that could be used to identify – the subject of the health information (known as an “identifier”) is protected only while it is maintained in a designated record set.

Whenever identifiers are maintained separately from individually identifiable health information, they are no longer Protected Health Information and the protections of the HIPAA Privacy Rule no longer apply. As an example, if a designated record set includes a patient’s diagnosis, their home telephone number, the name of their partner, and their healthcare payment details, all four elements of information are protected while they are maintained in the same designated record set.

If a separate record set is created containing a copy of the home telephone number and partner’s name (perhaps to provide the partner with an update on the patient’s health), these elements are not protected by the HIPAA Privacy Rule because there is no health information included in the record set. It is important to be aware that in such circumstances, although the HIPAA Rules do not apply, state privacy and security rules may.

How is Information Protected by the HIPAA Privacy Regulations?

The HIPAA Privacy Regulations, or “standards”, protect information by stipulating when uses and disclosures or Protected Health Information are required, permitted, or subject to an individual’s authorization. There are only two occasions when uses and disclosures are required; when an individual exercises their access rights and when access is required by HHS’ Office for Civil Rights for an investigation or compliance review. Both of these events are discussed in greater detail later.

Permissible uses and disclosures include those necessary to carry out treatment, payment, or health care operations, those required by law or for public health activities, and those necessary to avert a serious threat to health or safety. Among the disclosures permitted by HIPAA, there are some that are required by state laws. For example, disclosures to report abuse, neglect, or domestic abuse. Some “permissible” disclosures may also be “required” during emergency incidents.

Other than the uses and disclosures required or permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Regulations, and some for which the individual should be given an opportunity to object when feasible, all other uses and disclosures of Protected Health Information are prohibited unless they are authorized by the individual who is the subject of the Protected Health Information or their personal representative. Such uses and disclosures include uses for marketing and disclosures of psychotherapy notes.

Authorizations have to be written in clear language and explain to the individual what Protected Health Information is being used or disclosed, who to, and what for. If the covered entity is receiving a remuneration for the use or disclosure, this has to be included in the authorization, as does a warning that the covered entity may have no control over further disclosures of the Protected Health Information if, for example, it is published on a social media platform.

How do the HIPAA Privacy Standards Ensure Individuals’ Rights?

The HIPAA Privacy Standards ensure individuals’ rights by first requiring covered health plans and healthcare providers to give a HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices to new patients or plan members on the “first encounter” whenever possible or as soon as reasonable afterwards.

The Notice must describe the ways in which the covered entity may use or disclose Protected Health Information and describe how individuals can exercise their rights to access copies of their Protected Health Information.

The right to access copies of Protected Health Information is the “required” disclosure mentioned above, but it is important for individuals to understand they are only able to access information maintained in a designated record set.

It is also important to understand that complying with an access request may take some time when multiple designated record sets are maintained per individual, or when Protected Health Information is in the possession of a business associate.

Once an individual has received a copy of their Protected Health Information the HIPAA Privacy Standards allows individuals to request corrections to the information if it is inaccurate or incomplete.

Individuals can also request information is transferred to another provider, or that specific information is withheld from certain organizations. For example, if a patient has paid for treatment privately, they have the right to request this information is withheld from their insurer.

Individuals also have the right to request an accounting of disclosures. This document should contain a list of the times when Protected Health Information has been disclosed for reasons other than those permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Regulations or authorized by the individual themselves. Individuals have the right to query any entry on the accounting of disclosures and, if not satisfied with the response, make a complaint about their privacy rights being violated.

Who Enforces HIPAA Privacy Rules?

The Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights (OCR) is the enforcer of the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Noncompliance could lead to civil and criminal penalties, highlighting the importance of rigorous adherence.

What Happens if You Violate HIPAA Privacy Regulations?

The violation of privacy rights is one of the leading reasons for complaints to HHS’ Office for Civil Rights; and when a complaint is received by the agency, it has to be reviewed and investigated if it appears there has been a violation of HIPAA regulations.

When HHS’ Office for Civil Rights conducts an investigation, a covered entity must disclose whatever Protected Health Information is necessary for the agency to conclude its investigation – as mentioned previously in the section explaining how information is protected.

Most violations of HIPAA regulations are resolved by technical assistance or a corrective action plan. This means that the covered entity or business associate may have to develop and implement new policies and procedures to resolve the issue responsible for the violation of the HIPAA regulations. The organization may then have to train its workforce on the new policies and procedures and, depending on the scale of the violation(s), undergo a period of compliance monitoring.

In cases where there has been a willful neglect of the HIPAA regulations, HHS’ Office for Civil Rights has the authority to impose civil monetary penalties on noncompliant organizations. Historically, financial settlements and civil monetary penalties have been reserved for the worst offenders following large-scale data breaches. More recently, the agency has pursued a campaign to address violations of the HIPAA regulations that deny individuals their Privacy Rule rights.
