As well as organizations being penalized for non-compliance, members of the workforce can be sanctioned as well. The degree of sanction will depend on the nature of the violation and the content of the organization’s sanctions policy. In the worst cases of knowing and wrongful disclosures of PHI for personal gain, cases can be referred to the Department of Justice – who can pursue custodial sentences of up to ten years and fines of up to $250,000.

When was the Last Update to the HIPAA Privacy Rule?

The most recent update to the HIPAA Privacy Rule is the final rule HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens. The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) announced it on November 16, 2026, and it was published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. The update was a long time coming. HHS first proposed the changes in December 2020, and the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking was published in the Federal Register on January 21, 2021, almost six years before the final rule was issued.

What were the Major Changes Introduced by the Update?

The 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule update has three main aims: strengthening the individual right of access, making it easier to share information for care coordination, and reducing the administrative burden on covered entities. The final rule also adds definitions of “electronic health record” and “personal health application” to the Privacy Rule.

Changes to Patients’ Right of Access

The biggest change for most covered entities is the time allowed to respond to access requests. It has been cut from 30 days to 15 days. The option of one 30-day extension remains. Individuals can ask for copies of ePHI in a designated record set to be sent to a personal health application of their choice. Covered entities only have to do this if the ePHI is readily producible in that form. They don’t have to implement new technology to make it possible, but they must use technology they already have or that other laws require. Individuals can also direct a covered health care provider to send ePHI held in an electronic health record to a third party.

Covered entities can no longer charge individuals for inspecting their PHI in person or for accessing their ePHI through an internet-based method, such as a patient portal or a personal health app connected through an API. Access that involves workforce labor, such as emailing a PDF on request, is not considered internet-based, so a reasonable, cost-based fee may still be charged. For other types of access, fees are limited to:

  • labor for copying
  • supplies for non-electronic copies
  • postage
  • preparing a summary or explanation, if the individual agrees to it

Covered entities with a website must post a fee schedule on it and make the schedule available at the point of service. They are also encouraged to consider the financial circumstances of the person making the request. Covered entities must not impose unreasonable identity verification requirements. They also must not create barriers to access, such as accepting requests only through a patient portal.

Changes to Facilitate Better Care Coordination

The final rule expressly allows covered entities to disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management to third parties, such as social services agencies, community-based organizations, and home and community-based services providers. The minimum necessary standard still applies to these disclosures where relevant. A covered entity is not liable if the recipient later misuses or improperly discloses the information. The definition of health care operations has also been clarified to include care coordination and case management at both the individual and population level. This is particularly relevant to health plans.

Reducing the Administrative Burden

Covered health care providers no longer have to make a good faith effort to obtain written acknowledgment that a patient received the Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP). They also no longer have to document why an acknowledgment was not obtained. HHS estimates that this change alone will save around $798 million a year. Related changes to reduce the administrative burden include:

  • Disclosures to Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) communications assistants are permitted, and TRS providers are no longer considered business associates.
  • The permission to use and disclose the PHI of Armed Forces personnel for mission readiness now covers all uniformed services, including the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps and the NOAA Commissioned Corps.
Other Changes Introduced by the Update

Other changes introduced by the 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule update include that individuals have the right to discuss the content of the Notice of Privacy Practices (NPPs) with a designated contact, and NPPs must be updated to explain this new right. The NPP header must also refer to “health information” rather than “medical information.” The right to receive an NPP is also extended to inmates of correctional facilities that qualify as HIPAA covered entities.

Several proposals from the 2021 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking were not finalized. These include allowing individuals to take photographs of their PHI during in-person inspections, changing the standard for disclosures to family members and caregivers from “professional judgment” to “good faith,” and capping the fees that can be charged for sending copies of PHI to third parties.

How Long do HIPAA-Regulated Entities Have to Comply with the 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule Update?

The final rule takes effect on January 18, 2027, 60 days after it was published in the Federal Register. Covered entities and business associates then have a further 180 days to comply. The compliance date is July 17, 2027. After that date, OCR can enforce the new requirements and may impose civil monetary penalties for noncompliance. Until then, the current requirements still apply, including the 30-day timeframe for responding to access requests.

By the compliance date, covered entities need to update their policies and procedures, publish their access fee schedules, and retrain their workforces on the new requirements. They also need to have their revised NPPs available on their websites, posted at their facilities, and ready to give to new patients.

There is a longer transition period for business associate agreements. Existing agreements that comply with the current requirements will be deemed compliant until whichever of these comes first:

  • the agreement is renewed or modified after July 17, 2027
  • January 18, 2028

The same transition period applies to agreements between business associates and their subcontractors. Verbal arrangements are not covered by the transition provision.

HIPAA Privacy Rule Compliance Overview

To support HIPAA compliance efforts, the information in this article should be used in conjunction with our free, easy to use HIPAA Privacy Rule Checklist PDF which can be ordered by using any form on this page.

Privacy Rule HIPAA compliance necessitates organizational actions and technical precautions. Organizationally, covered entities and business associates must implement and enforce privacy policies and procedures in line with the HIPAA Privacy Rule.

A privacy official should be appointed to oversee the development and implementation of these policies. Regular training sessions must be held to familiarize workforce members with these guidelines.

Covered entities must also inform individuals about their privacy rights and the potential use of their information. A HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices should be readily available for anyone requesting it.

Breaches of unsecured PHI must be reported to the individuals affected, the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and in certain circumstances, to the media.

For instances where PHI needs to be shared, covered entities should create contracts ensuring that business associates will protect the information. These contracts, known as Business Associate Agreements (BAAs), are a critical part of Privacy Rule HIPAA compliance.

HIPAA Privacy Rule FAQs What are the eighteen identifiers that determine whether health information should be protected?

There is sometimes a misconception that the eighteen “HIPAA identifiers” listed under §164.514 of the HIPAA Privacy Rule are Protected Health Information at all times. This is not the case. These identifiers relate to the information that must be removed from a designated record set before any remaining health or payment information is considered de-identified under the safe harbor method.

As explained above, any identifier that is maintained in a designated record set along with health or payment information is protected while it is maintained in the same designated record set. When maintained in a database that does not contain health or payment information, identifiers are not protected by HIPAA, although state privacy and security laws may apply.

It is important to be aware that the list of eighteen HIPAA identifiers was compiled more than twenty years ago and has not been updated to reflect changes in how individuals can be identified. For example, if details of a patient’s emotional support animal are maintained in a designated record set, and the patient could be identified by the emotional support animal, these details also need to be removed from a designated record set before any remaining health information is de-identified.

In what circumstances can an individual object to disclosures of Protected Health Information?

These most often relate to disclosing information via a facility directory or notifying an individual’s family when (for example) an individual is admitted to hospital. Individuals can consent to limited information being disclosed in these circumstances or, if the individual is incapable of providing consent, covered entities can determine whether the disclosure is in the best interests of the individual. The information that can be disclosed in such circumstances is listed in §164.510.

What is the difference between individual consent and individual authorization?

For any other uses or disclosures of Protected Health Information other than those required or permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Rule, an individual has to give their consent or authorization. Consent, which can be verbal, is only allowed for the uses and disclosures included in §164.510. All other uses and disclosures require a written authorization signed by the individual. As a guideline, consent relates to obtaining permission for routine activities. Authorization is necessary when PHI is going to be used or disclosed for a non-routine activity.

What happens if you disclose Protected Health Information without an authorization?

If you disclose Protected Health Information impermissibly, it is a violation of HIPAA. The consequences of any HIPAA violation depend on various factors such as the nature of the violation, the harm to the individual, the organization’s sanctions policy, and the previous compliance history of both the person responsible for the violation and the organization they work for.

The impermissible disclosure of Protected Health Information may qualify as a data breach, in which case both the individual and HHS’ Office of Civil Rights need to be notified of the event. If the disclosure does not qualify as a data breach, the individual can still complain to HHS’ Office for Civil Rights, who may decide to investigate the organization depending on its compliance history.

What are the 3 Rules of HIPAA?

The three Rules of HIPAA that covered entities are required to comply with are the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the HIPAA Security Rule, and the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule which was introduced via the HITECH Act of 2009. There are two other Rules commonly associated with HIPAA; the HIPAA Enforcement Rule, which describes the process for compliance investigations, and the Omnibus HIPAA Final Rule which, in 2013, updated the HIPAA Privacy Rule and HIPAA Security Rule with other measures introduced by the HITECH Act.

In addition, it is important not to overlook the HIPAA General Provisions (Part 160, Subpart A) which explains many of the terms used in the HIPAA laws and regulations, and the Organization Requirements of Part 164 (§164.105) which explain which components of the HIPAA Privacy Rule apply to non-standard covered entities (i.e., Organized Health Care Arrangements, etc.). Covered entities and business associates are also required to comply with, or oversee compliance with, the Part 162 Rules relating to transactions and code sets.

What is the purpose of the Privacy Rule?

The purpose of the Privacy Rule is to set a federal floor of privacy protections for individuals’ individually identifiable health information. The Privacy Rule also gives individuals an opportunity to better control how their health information is used and disclosed, to take a more active role in their healthcare, and choose the best healthcare provider for their requirements.

Who is not covered by the HIPAA Privacy Rule?

Any organization that does not qualify as a covered entity or that does not provide a service for or on behalf of a covered entity as a business associate is not covered by the HIPAA Privacy Rule. It is important to be aware that business associates are only required to comply with the Privacy Rule “where provided”, and this is usually established in a Business Associate Agreement. Some business associates may not be covered by the HIPAA Privacy Rule depending on the service provided, and may only required to comply with the HIPAA Security and Breach Notification Rules.

When does the Privacy Rule not apply to health information?

The Privacy Rule does not apply to health information in a number of circumstances. These include when an organization does not qualify as a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, when the health information belongs to a student and is covered by FERPA, when other, more stringent, Rules than HIPAA apply, and when an individual has authorized a use or disclosure which may be subject to further uses and disclosures that a covered entity has no control over (i.e., when it is published on social media).

Why is the Privacy Rule important?

Research suggests when patients believe their health information is protected, they are more willing to discuss intimate details with healthcare providers. With more information, healthcare providers can make more accurate diagnoses and prescribe more effective courses of treatment, leading to better patient outcomes, higher morale in the workplace, and increased hospital satisfaction scores.

What are HIPAA Rules and why are they different?

The HIPAA Rules are the standards within the Administrative Simplification Regulations that govern how covered entities must protect the privacy of Protected Health Information, how electronic Protected Health Information should be safeguarded to ensure its confidentiality, integrity, and availability, and how covered entities should respond in the event of an impermissible use or disclosure or a data breach.

The reason they may be considered “different” is that they are a baseline of privacy and security standards. In many states, more stringent privacy and/or security standards, or regulations providing individuals with greater access rights, overlay parts of HIPAA. Some states also have privacy and security standards that cross borders, protecting the individually identifiable health information of state residents wherever they are in the United States.

What is the difference between the Privacy Rule of HIPAA, the HIPAA Privacy Law, and the HIPAA Privacy Act?

There is no difference between the Privacy Rule of HIPAA, the HIPAA Privacy Law, and the HIPAA Privacy Act. These are names sometimes used to describe the “Standards for the Privacy of Individual Identifiable Health Information” published in Subpart E of Part 164 of the HIPAA Administrative Simplification Regulations.

Most sources, including the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights, refer to the Standards as the “HIPAA Privacy Rule” to avoid confusing the agency-promulgated standards with Laws or Acts passed by Congress. For example, the HIPAA Act was passed by Congress, but the HIPAA Rules were promulgated by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

items.title: Worries About Rogue AI Agents And The Cost Of Cybercrime
items.summary: This week in cybersecurity from the editors at Cybercrime Magazine Sausalito, Calif. – Nov. 18, 2026
items.summary_html:
This week in cybersecurity from the editors at Cybercrime Magazine

Sausalito, Calif. – Nov. 18, 2026

– Read the Full Story in LinkedIn

Rogue AI agents steal the headlines, but the bigger damage right now comes from criminals using AI for fraud, says Ken Elefant, Managing Director, Ventures at Sorenson Capital, in a LinkedIn article.

Cybercrime already costs an estimated $10.5 trillion a year, according to Cybersecurity Ventures, and mid-sized companies and their managed service providers (MSPs) are taking the hardest hit, getting buried in business email compromise, deepfake hiring scams, and ransomware.

This past summer, some 700 OpenAI agents broke out of a sealed testing sandbox and spent several days inside Hugging Face’s production infrastructure hunting for the answers to a cybersecurity benchmark. Once they got what they were looking for, many of them tried to erase any clues they’d been there in the first place.

Elefant understands why the AI doom crowd is having a bit of a moment. But that’s not the AI risk he hears about most. He spends most of his week with security founders and the CISOs who buy from them. When AI comes up, rogue agents are rarely first, or even third. What comes up is criminals using the same AI tools to steal money from companies that don’t have anyone watching.

You can quibble with the cybercrime damage cost figures, but even if you haircut that number hard, the order of magnitude doesn’t change. If cybercrime were a country, it would be the third largest economy in the world, behind only the U.S. and China, and growing at roughly 15 percent a year.

The reported numbers echo that. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) logged more than one million complaints in 2025, and that’s just what got reported. Cybersecurity Ventures estimates that fewer than a quarter of cybercrimes globally ever get reported to law enforcement.

items.title: Healthcare Employees Sharing Patient Data with AI Tools Viewed as Major Emerging Risk
items.summary: Healthcare security leaders are increasingly concerned about patient privacy incidents, HIPAA violations, and intellectual property loss due to employees sharing sensitive data with public AI models. While there is a risk of employees uploading patient data to unapproved tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, sensitive data may also be disclosed by unauthorized browser extensions, plug-ins, or an OAuth grant, which can be approved in a few clicks. According to a recent survey by the cybersecurity company DNS Filter, 43% of healthcare security leaders said they believe employee sharing of sensitive data with AI models is the biggest emerging AI risk in the next 12 months. The biggest perceived risk is loss of intellectual property through AI training data, rated as the biggest risk by 53% of respondents, compared to 31% in other sectors. Multiple privacy incidents have already been reported by healthcare providers involving employees uploading sensitive patient data to public AI models, in violation of their organization’s data privacy and security policies and the HIPAA Rules. Recent examples include Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center , Weill Cornell Medicine, and the Washington Department of Social and Health Services . Since breaches of protected health information are only made public via the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights breach portal if they affect 500 or more individuals, and media notices are only required for breaches of that magnitude, the problem could be far more extensive. The DNSFilter survey findings suggest that may well be the case. Around half of healthcare respondents have either confirmed (27%) or suspect (23%) that employees have connected an unapproved AI tool to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or their SSO environment. While patient data may not have been involved in those actual or suspected incidents, it is a significant risk, and a lack of AI governance means privacy violations may go unnoticed. According to the DNSFilter report – Seeing the Risk, Missing the Signal: AI Security in Healthcare – only 27% of respondents said every security tool they own is actively monitored, and 40% of respondents said they actively monitor 50% or fewer security tools. While 70% of organizations confirmed they have implemented formal policies prohibiting the use of unapproved AI tools, only 40% said their policy is consistently enforced. Half of respondents said AI security and governance is one of their biggest security gaps; the highest share of any sector. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Six out of 10 respondents said they are reliant on their AI and SaaS vendors to alert them to security incidents, which is more than the 43% of respondents from other sectors. Only 23% of healthcare respondents said they catch SaaS and AI incidents through employee reporting, compared to 44% in other sectors. An additional concern is that 47% of healthcare organizations said their employer can authorize a new AI tool to access company systems without higher-level approval. Despite the security gaps, confidence is high in the ability to detect breaches. In healthcare, 87% of respondents said they are confident that they could detect a breach within 6 hours, and 40% said they are very confident. One-third said they had experienced an incident that originated from a SaaS or AI tool in the past 12 months, and the same percentage said they had experienced such an incident that was never formally reported or disclosed. Despite the risks, only a small percentage of healthcare organizations rate AI security and governance as one of the most important areas for IT security spending. Only 33% of respondents said they are sending their next dollar to AI security and governance, compared to 41% in other industries. This shows that while concern about risk is growing, money to address the problem is not following. “Healthcare security leaders know exactly where AI puts their data at risk. What they’re missing is the moment that risk becomes an incident, and too many are hearing about it from a vendor instead of their own team. When the data involved is protected health information, the risk only becomes more significant. Before the next dollar goes to AI governance, healthcare organizations need to see which AI services their people are already using without clearance,” said Ken Carnesi, CEO, DNSFilter.

items.title: Fraudsters Scam 500K Viewers with Fake Tesla Flying Car Livestream Giveaway
items.summary: AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk used in crypto scam targeting 500,000 viewers, with Rs 42 crore in estimated losses. The Deepfake Scam Incident Fraudsters exploited an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk to conduct a cryptocurrency scam targeting approximately 500,000 viewers, with estimated losses reaching Rs 42 crore. The scheme involved a fabricated livestream promoting a non-existent Tesla flying car demonstration, which enticed participants with promises of doubling their cryptocurrency investments. Methods Used by Fraudsters The operation leveraged artificial intelligence to create a convincing broadcast, displaying cryptocurrency wallet addresses and QR codes to direct users toward fraudulent transactions. The fraudulent livestream, which lasted approximately two hours, featured a high-fidelity AI-generated video of Musk that mimicked authentic corporate messaging. The content included visual elements such as cryptocurrency wallet addresses and QR codes, accompanied by instructions for users to send funds under the guise of a limited-time opportunity. Coinbase’s AI Defense Mechanisms A security system developed by cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase intercepted the majority of these attempts, blocking 91% of suspicious transfers before significant damage occurred. Over 500,000 individuals tuned into the stream, with hundreds of Coinbase users initiating transactions totaling millions of dollars before the platform’s safeguards activated. Multi-Layered AI Response Coinbase deployed a multi-layered AI defense mechanism to counter the threat. The first layer involved real-time monitoring of transactions flagged as suspicious, triggering automatic alerts. The second phase engaged an AI-powered communication system to educate users about the nature of cryptocurrency giveaway scams, highlighting the risks associated with transferring funds to unverified addresses. A third component assigned confidence scores to each response generated by the AI, ensuring the system’s assessments aligned with established fraud detection protocols. Notably, the AI identified the scheme without prior training on deepfake-based product launch scams, recognizing patterns such as exaggerated return guarantees and artificial urgency. Evolving Trends in Deepfake Fraud This incident underscores a growing trend in deepfake-enabled financial fraud, where high-profile figures are increasingly impersonated to exploit public trust. Similar AI-generated videos featuring Musk emerged in 2024, promoting fraudulent investment opportunities and giveaways. Deepfakes of other prominent individuals, including Warren Buffett and Jeff Bezos, have also been used in recent scams. Accessibility of Deepfake Technology The declining cost and increasing speed of deepfake production enable fraudsters to disseminate deceptive content rapidly across social media and paid advertisements, amplifying their reach. Coinbase’s Response and Warnings Coinbase has intensified its focus on AI-driven fraud detection, investing in advanced research to identify emerging scam methodologies. The exchange reiterated its warning to users that legitimate entities never request cryptocurrency transfers in exchange for guaranteed returns. It emphasized that no verified organization would ask for funds via wallet addresses or QR codes displayed in videos, livestreams, or messages. Conclusion: Combating AI-Powered Fraud The incident highlights the evolving challenges of combating AI-powered fraud, as threat actors leverage cutting-edge technology to bypass traditional security measures. Enterprises and financial institutions are increasingly reliant on AI-based systems to detect and mitigate such threats, while user education remains a critical component of cybersecurity strategy. As deepfake technology becomes more accessible, the need for robust detection frameworks and public awareness campaigns grows imperative to safeguard against increasingly sophisticated scams.

items.title: British Scattered Spider Hacker Gets 6-Year Prison Sentence
items.summary: British Scattered Spider hacker sentenced to 6 years in prison Sentencing and Charges A senior member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime network has received a six-year prison term in the United States for orchestrating cryptocurrency theft and phishing campaigns targeting multiple organizations. Defendant Details 24-year-old Tyler Robert Buchanan from the United Kingdom was charged in November 2024 along with four others for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft linked to phishing operations between September 2021 and April 2023. Targeted Sectors The group targeted entities across diverse sectors, including telecommunications, technology, business process outsourcing (BPO), entertainment, and information technology (IT) suppliers. Attacks also affected virtual currency platforms, cloud communications providers, and individual users. Phishing Tactics The perpetrators deployed SMS-based phishing messages to employees of victim companies, impersonating internal teams or third-party IT or BPO vendors. These messages directed recipients to counterfeit websites designed to mimic legitimate corporate portals, tricking them into divulging sensitive data such as login credentials and personally identifiable information. Financial Impact The stolen data facilitated the unauthorized transfer of over $11.6 million in digital assets by compromising cryptocurrency accounts and wallets. Prosecutors emphasized the extensive harm caused by the scheme, noting its “severe, life-altering consequences” for victims. Evidence Recovery In April 2023, law enforcement recovered a device at Buchanan’s residence in Scotland containing victim details, including a text file with cryptocurrency seed phrases and login credentials for one affected account. Apprehension and Sentencing Buchanan was apprehended in Palma de Mallorca, Spain, in June 2024, and has been held in U.S. federal custody since April 2025. He pleaded guilty to cryptocurrency theft charges in April 2025. Co-Conspirators Three co-conspirators—Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy, and Joel Martin Evans—were also charged in November 2024 with wire fraud and identity theft. They received multi-year sentences after pleading guilty. Another key member, Noah Michael Urban (known online as Sosa and Elijah), was sentenced to 10 years in prison for similar offenses in April 2025. Group Operations The Scattered Spider collective, also known by aliases such as 0ktapus and UNC3944, operates through encrypted communication platforms like Telegram and Discord. The group has collaborated with Russian ransomware operations, including BlackCat/AlphV, Qilin, and RansomHub, since early 2023. Law Enforcement Response FBI reports highlight their use of social engineering, multi-factor authentication (MFA) fatigue attacks, phishing, and SIM swapping to breach corporate networks. Some members have also been associated with “The Com,” a separate hacking group linked to violent cyber incidents. The case underscores the growing threat of organized cybercrime and the financial devastation caused by sophisticated phishing schemes. Law enforcement agencies continue to track and dismantle networks exploiting digital vulnerabilities for illicit gain. items.summary_html:
British Scattered Spider hacker sentenced to 6 years in prison

Sentencing and Charges

A senior member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime network has received a six-year prison term in the United States for orchestrating cryptocurrency theft and phishing campaigns targeting multiple organizations.

Defendant Details

24-year-old Tyler Robert Buchanan from the United Kingdom was charged in November 2024 along with four others for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft linked to phishing operations between September 2021 and April 2023.

Targeted Sectors

The group targeted entities across diverse sectors, including telecommunications, technology, business process outsourcing (BPO), entertainment, and information technology (IT) suppliers. Attacks also affected virtual currency platforms, cloud communications providers, and individual users.

Phishing Tactics

The perpetrators deployed SMS-based phishing messages to employees of victim companies, impersonating internal teams or third-party IT or BPO vendors. These messages directed recipients to counterfeit websites designed to mimic legitimate corporate portals, tricking them into divulging sensitive data such as login credentials and personally identifiable information.

Financial Impact

The stolen data facilitated the unauthorized transfer of over $11.6 million in digital assets by compromising cryptocurrency accounts and wallets. Prosecutors emphasized the extensive harm caused by the scheme, noting its “severe, life-altering consequences” for victims.

Evidence Recovery

In April 2023, law enforcement recovered a device at Buchanan’s residence in Scotland containing victim details, including a text file with cryptocurrency seed phrases and login credentials for one affected account.

Apprehension and Sentencing

Buchanan was apprehended in Palma de Mallorca, Spain, in June 2024, and has been held in U.S. federal custody since April 2025. He pleaded guilty to cryptocurrency theft charges in April 2025.

Co-Conspirators

Three co-conspirators—Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy, and Joel Martin Evans—were also charged in November 2024 with wire fraud and identity theft. They received multi-year sentences after pleading guilty. Another key member, Noah Michael Urban (known online as Sosa and Elijah), was sentenced to 10 years in prison for similar offenses in April 2025.

Group Operations

The Scattered Spider collective, also known by aliases such as 0ktapus and UNC3944, operates through encrypted communication platforms like Telegram and Discord. The group has collaborated with Russian ransomware operations, including BlackCat/AlphV, Qilin, and RansomHub, since early 2023.

Law Enforcement Response

FBI reports highlight their use of social engineering, multi-factor authentication (MFA) fatigue attacks, phishing, and SIM swapping to breach corporate networks. Some members have also been associated with “The Com,” a separate hacking group linked to violent cyber incidents.

The case underscores the growing threat of organized cybercrime and the financial devastation caused by sophisticated phishing schemes. Law enforcement agencies continue to track and dismantle networks exploiting digital vulnerabilities for illicit gain.

Conclusion

The sentencing of Tyler Robert Buchanan highlights the global reach of cybercrime networks and the severe penalties for those involved in cryptocurrency theft and phishing operations. As cyber threats evolve, coordinated international efforts remain critical to combating digital fraud and protecting organizations and individuals from financial harm.

items.title: Alleged U.S Hospital Ransomware Attacker Extradited to U.S. to Face Charges
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice has announced that a Kazakh national suspected of engaging in ransomware attacks on U.S. hospitals, healthcare organizations, and schools has been extradited to the U.S. to face charges. Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, is alleged to have been a member of the 8-Digits Team, a ransomware group with links to the INC Ransom and Lynx ransomware groups. Along with other members of the 8-Digits Team, Khlynovskiy is alleged to have repeatedly targeted schools, hospitals, and other healthcare providers in at least six U.S. states. Khlynovskiy is alleged to have breached protected networks, exfiltrated data, and encrypted files. Victims were threatened with publication of the stolen data to pressure them into paying ransoms. According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), 8-Digits Team claimed to have exfiltrated more than 50 terabytes of sensitive data, including more than 70 million private and confidential health records, threatened to publish the data, and demanded at least $500 million in ransom payments. Khlynovskiy travelled to Rimini, Italy, in July 2025 for a family vacation and was arrested and detained by Italian authorities. He was recently extradited to the United States and has been formally charged with conspiracy to commit computer fraud and identity theft, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, extortion involving computers, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and threats to disclose nonconsensual intimate images in violation of the TAKE IT DOWN Act. The TAKE IT DOWN Act criminalizes the non-consensual online publication of intimate images and was signed into law in May 2025. Khlynovskiy made his initial appearance in federal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on November 16, 2026. Khlynovskiy is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. If he is convicted on all counts, Khlynovskiy faces a maximum penalty of 27 years in jail. The FBI is committed to bringing ransomware attackers and other cybercriminals to the United States to face charges for their crimes. According to FBI Director Kash Patel, those efforts are among the most aggressive work the agency has conducted to bring fugitives to the United States. In the past 12 months, there have been 84 Foreign Transfers of Custody (FTOCs), an increase of 71%, and 157 extraditions, an increase of 121%. “Those who victimize Americans cannot evade justice by operating overseas, and the FBI will continue to pursue them wherever they may be,” said Patel. items.title: Microsoft Unveils Windows Server 2028 with Enhanced Security Features – New Release
items.summary: Microsoft has unveiled Windows Server 2028, the latest iteration of its server operating system, during the Ignite 2026 conference. Introduction to Windows Server 2028 Microsoft has unveiled Windows Server 2028, the latest iteration of its server operating system, during the Ignite 2026 conference. This release introduces a fortified Server Core configuration as the default setup, alongside a revised security baseline designed to streamline initial security configurations. Neil Hinnant, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM, emphasized that these updates aim to minimize the effort required to establish a secure environment from the outset. Security Enhancements \\\”Trusted Launch enhances protection for virtual machines by ensuring boot integrity across VM clusters, while Confidential VM capabilities mark the beginning of support for integrity-protected runtimes on compatible CVM hardware,\\\” he stated. Hardened Server Core Settings The hardened Server Core settings encompass multiple security layers, including identity and authentication measures such as Kerberos over NTLM, protected LSASS, robust password policies, and restrictions on consumer accounts. Network Exposure Mitigation Network exposure is mitigated through mandatory signed, encrypted, and authenticated communication channels, with SMB signing and encryption enabled, firewalls active across all profiles, and legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC disabled. Cryptographic Protocols Cryptographic protocols prioritize modern TLS cipher suites, hybrid post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM), and enhanced protection for stored cryptographic keys. Privilege Management Privilege management features require administrative approval for elevation, restrict powerful rights to the Administrators group, and prevent guest logins or self-elevating installer actions. Platform Integrity Platform integrity ensures only Microsoft-signed code executes during sign-in, with stricter signature validation and encrypted paging files. Remote Access Controls Remote access controls mandate RDP with NLA and TLS, secure WinRM configurations, and advanced auditing with command-line tracking, PowerShell script block logging, and expanded event logs. Performance and Administration Improvements Despite these advancements, the company acknowledged ongoing work to implement NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, print and RPC hardening, and additional security settings. Windows Server 2028 also introduces simplified administration via Intune integration, enabling endpoint management workflows for configuration, compliance, applications, and updates on eligible servers. Performance Enhancements Performance enhancements include native NVMe storage support, NVMe over TCP and RDMA transports, and boot capability from ReFS. AI Integration and Accelerators The release further integrates AI accelerators, allowing deployment of inference environments, management of accelerated hardware, and support for open-weight and custom models such as Windows ML, Foundry Local, vLLM, and Llama.cpp. Quotes from Neil Hinnant \\\”It also initiates long-term investments to extend Microsoft Foundry, enabling AI inference on local token factories and providing customers with flexible intelligence deployment options,\\\” he added. Conclusion Hinnant highlighted that this update elevates security standards, accelerates enterprise infrastructure, and simplifies large-scale management.

items.title: Critical Apache Roller RCE Vulnerability Exploited in Active Attacks
items.summary: Apache has issued security patches to resolve a critical flaw in Apache Roller, which attackers are leveraging to achieve remote code execution on affected servers. Understanding the Vulnerability The open-source Java-based group-blogging platform, though less widely used than modern content management systems, is under active exploitation due to the vulnerability. The flaw, designated CVE-2026-129448, enables unauthenticated adversaries to execute arbitrary code by exploiting deserialization of untrusted data through the XML-RPC endpoint. Impact and Affected Versions This vulnerability affects all versions from 4.0.0 to 6.1.4, with the exploit chain involving the acceptance and deserialization of vendor extension types prior to authentication. Apache confirmed this issue overlaps with CVE-2026-82384, which previously impacted only version 6.1.5, but now remains actively targeted. Mitigation and Recommendations Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables extension types and blocks malicious XML-RPC requests by deactivating the XML-RPC feature. Administrators unable to apply updates immediately can implement temporary fixes by setting “enabledForExtensions” to “false” in the WEB-INF/web.xml file, removing the “/roller-services/xmlrpc” servlet mapping, and restarting the service. Disabling XML-RPC via the administrative interface alone is insufficient, as older versions process requests before verifying this setting. Broader Trends in Exploited Software Flaws The vulnerability aligns with broader trends of exploited software flaws, including recent alerts from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). In April, CISA highlighted a 13-year-old Apache ActiveMQ vulnerability (CVE-2026-34197) as actively exploited, mandating federal agencies to address it within two weeks. Recent Apache Security Updates Additionally, Apache recently resolved a critical HTTP/2 module flaw in its server software, which allowed remote code execution on unpatched systems. Since November 2021, CISA has documented 41 Apache vulnerabilities in its catalog of actively exploited flaws, with eight linked to ransomware operations. Conclusion The flaw underscores the persistent risks associated with legacy systems and the importance of timely patching. Organizations using Apache Roller must prioritize updates to prevent unauthorized access and potential data breaches. Technical teams should also review their XML-RPC configurations and ensure all components are hardened against known exploitation vectors.

items.title: Dizigom Unauthorized Streaming Service Closes After 21M Monthly Visits
items.summary: The Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE) has confirmed the closure of Dizigom, a prominent piracy platform based in Turkey, following a mutual agreement with its administrators. Investigation and Resolution The investigation into Dizigom’s operations commenced in 2023, with Turkish law enforcement collaborating to trace the platform’s operators and their digital infrastructure. As part of the resolution, the administrators consented to discontinue the service, surrender control of 16 domains to ACE, and ensure the platform’s permanent removal from the internet. Coordinated Effort with Authorities A coordinated effort involving INTERPOL and Turkish authorities led to the settlement, which includes the redirection of Dizigom’s domains to ACE’s “Watch Legally” initiative. This portal educates users on accessing authorized streaming options. ACE’s Role in Combating Piracy ACE, an organization representing over 50 major entertainment entities such as Disney, Warner Bros., Netflix, and Paramount, has prioritized dismantling illicit streaming networks through legal actions, criminal referrals, and enforcement operations. The coalition has previously collaborated with global law enforcement agencies, including Europol, the U.S. Department of Justice, and Interpol, to target large-scale piracy operations. Larissa Knapp, Executive Vice President and Chief Content Protection Officer at the Motion Picture Association, emphasized the importance of disrupting piracy networks. “By exposing the individuals and systems behind these services, we can dismantle the infrastructure that enables their continued existence,” she stated. “This case underscores the effectiveness of partnerships with Turkish authorities and the persistent efforts required to hold operators responsible.” Recent Takedowns and Milestones ACE’s recent actions include the takedown of AnimePlay, a major anime streaming site with over 5 million users, and the dismantling of a piracy ecosystem centered around the CINEMAGOAL app, which provided access to platforms like Netflix, Disney+, and Spotify. Additionally, the coalition reported the shutdown of a sports piracy operation linked to PirloTV, which managed 44 domains generating over 950 million annual visits. Conclusion The closure of Dizigom marks another milestone in ongoing efforts to combat digital piracy, reflecting the growing collaboration between industry groups and law enforcement to protect intellectual property and ensure compliance with legal streaming frameworks. FAQs No FAQs provided in the content.

items.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability Exploit Allows Unauthorized Access to Java Servers
items.summary: Oracle has addressed a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK that allows threat actors to execute arbitrary code on affected systems without authentication. Vulnerability Details The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, impacts hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding in specific Java runtime environments. Researchers identified the issue in the way Java processes binary data through text-based encoding, which can lead to memory corruption under certain conditions. Root Cause The vulnerability arises from improper handling of malformed input in the Base64 decoding process. On compatible processors, Java employs optimized instructions to speed up this operation. However, maliciously crafted data can trigger these accelerated routines to write beyond allocated memory buffers. Impact and Severity While the Java runtime ultimately rejects invalid input, the memory corruption may expose sensitive information or enable remote code execution. Security assessments assign the flaw a critical CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, while Oracle’s internal rating under CVSS 3.1 places it at 8.1. Scoring Discrepancy The discrepancy in scoring stems from differences in the evaluation frameworks used. Both metrics highlight the severity of the issue, noting high attack complexity and no requirement for user interaction or authentication. Affected Systems Affected systems include Java versions with specific runtime configurations. The vulnerability is active in Java 17 (17.0.6 through 17.0.21), Java 21 (through 21.0.13), Java 25 (through 25.0.5), Java 27 (through 27.0.1), and Java 8 Performance Pack (8u511b33-perf). Unaffected Systems Systems using Java 8, Java 11, or earlier versions of Java 17 (before 17.0.6) are not impacted by this particular flaw. Processor Architecture Processor architecture plays a key role in exposure. The vulnerable decoding mechanism relies on AVX-512 VBMI instructions available on x86-64 chips, while ARM64 processors remain unaffected. Mitigation Steps Organizations must also verify Java runtimes embedded in applications and container images, as standalone system updates may not address bundled versions. Temporary mitigation steps include disabling hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding via JVM flags such as -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 systems. Expert Recommendations Administrators are advised to test these changes with application vendors before deployment. Experts caution that while the vulnerability is severe, the reported exploits are not universally applicable. Expert Opinions Dom Glavach, chief information security officer at Black Duck, noted that the researchers have not provided public exploit chains and urged organizations to prioritize critical systems such as identity management and build servers. He also warned against relying on unverified patches or third-party exploits circulating online. Quote “The researchers have not provided public exploit chains and urged organizations to prioritize critical systems such as identity management and build servers.” Long-Term Strategies The flaw underscores the importance of timely patch management and runtime configuration reviews. Enterprises should verify their Java environments, apply updates, and monitor for signs of exploitation. The incident highlights ongoing risks associated with optimized code paths in widely used software frameworks. Conclusion The vulnerability affects systems where hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding is enabled. Organizations must ensure all Java runtimes, including those embedded in applications and containers, are updated to mitigate risks. Long-term strategies should focus on reducing reliance on complex optimization features that may introduce security trade-offs.

items.title: NSA Classified Network Down: Defense Official Confirms Outage
items.summary: A classified internal network used by the National Security Agency for secure communications experienced an outage on Tuesday, attributed by the agency to “routine maintenance.” NSA Outage Details A classified internal network used by the National Security Agency for secure communications experienced an outage on Tuesday, attributed by the agency to “routine maintenance.” The disruption affected NSANet, a system critical for internal operations, according to a defense official who spoke to The Associated Press under anonymity. The NSA confirmed the temporary operational degradation during scheduled maintenance, emphasizing that mission-critical functions remained unaffected. The agency stated its infrastructure incorporates redundancy measures to ensure continuity during planned or unplanned disruptions. No further details were provided regarding the cause or extent of the outage. Broader Context of Technical Failures This incident coincided with a series of technical failures across government and private sector systems in recent days. A system overload on Friday led to a nationwide air traffic ground stop in the United States, while JPMorgan Chase faced a technical issue on Monday that impacted financial operations. United Airlines also reported an internal systems outage causing flight delays. On Tuesday, Apple disclosed service disruptions for Apple Music, the App Store, and AppleCare following an internal update. Official Statements and Analysis U.S. officials downplayed concerns about malicious activity, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as the Trump administration’s national security adviser, stating there was no evidence linking the incidents to cyber threats, criminal actors, or foreign nations. Rubio acknowledged the frequency of technical failures as “unsettling” but reiterated that government and private entities remain vigilant. Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, attributed the disruptions to simultaneous system upgrades by government agencies and corporations. He noted that legacy systems often struggle with compatibility during modernization efforts, leading to temporary operational challenges. “Many organizations are patching their systems,” Clayton said in a CNBC interview, stressing the necessity of modernizing digital infrastructure to address vulnerabilities. Implications for System Resilience Sens. Mark Warner, a Democratic member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, highlighted the role of artificial intelligence in accelerating vulnerability identification, creating pressure for rapid system updates. “The pace of change is straining systems not designed to handle such demands,” Warner stated, adding that current evidence points to legitimate security efforts rather than malicious intent. items.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: Enterprise Applications at Risk of Security Threats
items.summary: Oracle and the OpenJDK project have addressed a critical vulnerability in the Java runtime environment known as Java4Shell, designated CVE-2026-114938. Overview Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938 Security Vulnerability Overview Oracle and the OpenJDK project have addressed a critical vulnerability in the Java runtime environment known as Java4Shell. Researchers identified the flaw, designated CVE-2026-114938, as a memory safety issue within the OpenJDK Base64 decoding process. The vulnerability arises from improper handling of Base64-encoded data on x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. A researcher named Quang Luong from Calif disclosed the issue publicly on November 17, following coordinated release of details. The flaw exists in a routine responsible for Base64 decoding, where malformed input can trigger buffer overflow conditions. This allows unauthorized memory corruption, potentially exposing sensitive data or enabling remote code execution. Discovery and Disclosure The researchers named the exploit vector JavaBleed, highlighting its similarity to the Heartbleed vulnerability. They emphasized that exposed heap data could contain personally identifiable information, cryptographic keys, and authentication tokens. Default configurations of several enterprise applications were found vulnerable to exploitation. Testing by Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate when running with default settings. “The researchers named the exploit vector JavaBleed, highlighting its similarity to the Heartbleed vulnerability.” Exploitation Details Authenticated attackers could also achieve code execution on Apache Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Additional proof-of-concept tests confirmed exploitation against applications built on Apache Struts and Spring Boot frameworks. The vulnerability can be triggered through standard application features such as authentication mechanisms and file uploads. Client-side attacks are possible when Java applications establish TLS connections to malicious servers. A proof-of-concept exploit shared by security researcher samczsun showed that compromising a Java application requires an attacker-controlled server to intercept legitimate traffic. The researchers noted that exploitation paths vary depending on application architecture and Base64 implementation. VulnCheck reported that crashing vulnerable Java Virtual Machines is straightforward once an attacker identifies a reachable decoding entry point. Their tests demonstrated that crafted requests could reliably disrupt services. “The company stated that weaponized exploits for individual products will remain confidential until all affected systems have received updates.” Affected Versions and Hardware The discovery and exploitation of the vulnerability involved artificial intelligence tools, according to Calif. The researcher reported that identifying the flaw and developing an initial exploit took approximately three hours, with total computational costs under $200. Affected versions include OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, along with distributions such as Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, Red Hat OpenJDK, and Oracle Java SE. The OpenJDK advisory lists Java versions 17, 21, 25, and 27 as vulnerable. Exploitation requires x86-64 hardware with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon processors from the Ice Lake generation or newer AMD chips based on Zen 4 architecture. ARM64-based systems are not affected. The vulnerability carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, while Oracle’s advisory assigns a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. The flaw is classified as remotely exploitable without authentication but requires high attack complexity. Recommendations and Mitigation Oracle included fixes in its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update, addressing 11 Java SE vulnerabilities. Endor Labs warned that users of alternative Java distributions must await vendor-specific patches. As of November 17, official OpenJDK 17, 21, and 25 update repositories had not yet included the fix. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued urgent recommendations for immediate patching, prioritizing internet-facing systems. The agency also advised searching for Java installations embedded in third-party software, containerized environments, and hardware appliances, which may not appear in standard asset inventories. Cisco Talos has not observed active exploitation in the wild but warned that reconnaissance activities could increase following public disclosure. Conclusion The vulnerability affects enterprise applications relying on Base64 decoding functionality. Researchers emphasized that exploitation requires specific hardware configurations and application-specific conditions. The discovery highlights ongoing challenges in securing widely used software components. Organizations are urged to apply available patches and conduct thorough system audits to identify potential exposure. Security teams should monitor for suspicious activity related to Java processes and implement network segmentation to limit potential attack surfaces. The incident underscores the importance of timely vulnerability management and proactive threat hunting in enterprise environments.

items.title: Critical Perforce Puppet RCE Vulnerability Exploited in Cyber Attacks
items.summary: Threat actors have been exploiting a high-risk vulnerability in Perforce Puppet, enabling unauthorized code execution on affected servers. Vulnerability Overview Perforce Puppet, a platform used for infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and system configuration management, operates through a client-server model for device control. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 with a CVSS score of 9.4, stems from a deserialization vulnerability in the report processing component of Puppet Enterprise and Puppet Core. Exploit Mechanics This defect allows attackers with valid certificates issued by the Puppet certificate authority (CA) to inject malicious payloads that execute on the server with elevated privileges, compromising managed systems. Perforce’s advisory highlights that a successful exploit could expose the server’s certificate-signing key, enabling adversaries to generate trusted certificates and alter software or configurations delivered during subsequent Puppet runs. Mitigation Measures The vulnerability arises when the CA automatically approves certificate requests without rigorous validation, granting unauthenticated attackers the ability to obtain credentials. Administrators are urged to disable auto-signing and implement strict validation protocols to ensure only authorized entities receive certificates. Impact and Exploitation The flaw was addressed on November 3, alongside another critical issue, CVE-2026-115732, which allowed attackers to bypass authorization by using certificates with names that match approved patterns. Patches for both vulnerabilities are included in Puppet Enterprise and Puppet Enterprise Advanced versions 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1, and 2023.8.13, as well as Puppet Core versions 9.1.3 and 8.22.2. Active Exploitation CVE-2026-115731 was identified as actively exploited starting November 4, prompting the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 17. Federal agencies were directed to apply patches within two weeks, aligning with guidelines from BOD 26-04. Additional Affected Systems The vulnerability also impacts the OpenVox configuration management platform. A proof-of-concept exploit targeting OpenVox was released shortly after the patch for CVE-2026-115731 became available. Security Recommendations Security researchers emphasize the urgency of addressing these flaws, as their exploitation could lead to widespread system compromises. Organizations using affected software are advised to review their certificate management practices and apply updates promptly to prevent potential breaches. “Organizations using affected software are advised to review their certificate management practices and apply updates promptly to prevent potential breaches.” Patched Versions Puppet Enterprise and Puppet Enterprise Advanced versions 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1, and 2023.8.13 Puppet Core versions 9.1.3 and 8.22.2

items.title: Microsoft Agent Framework Compromised by Credential Stealer
items.summary: Threat actors deployed two compromised iterations of the Microsoft Agent Framework Python package through the Python Package Index (PyPI) in a supply chain attack on November 17, exposing cloud and CI/CD credentials for users who installed the malicious versions. Overview of the Attack The Agent Framework, a tool for building AI agents and multi-agent systems, saw its affected package, agent-framework, distributed with approximately 190,000 downloads. The malicious releases, version 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart before being quarantined on PyPI. Version 1.26.0 remains the last verified clean release. Malicious Code Analysis The malicious code retained core framework components while embedding additional modules designed to extract credentials. This allowed compromised applications to function normally, masking the attack. Security researchers from OX Security, Wiz, Endor Labs, and SafeDep analyzed the malware, which leverages Python’s startup mechanisms to execute automatically whenever the interpreter runs, even without explicit package imports. Execution Mechanisms The payload targets secrets stored in environment variables, configuration files, and credentials from running processes. It also attempts to harvest Azure managed identity tokens and Azure DevOps authentication tokens, granting access to cloud infrastructure. A subsequent update expanded the theft capabilities to include GitHub Actions. Deployment and Investigation The method of deployment remains under investigation. Unlike legitimate releases, the malicious packages contained only built distributions, omitting source code. Wiz confirmed no corresponding malicious code existed in Microsoft’s official source repositories, suggesting the packages bypassed standard release channels. Maintainer Account Discovery SafeDep identified a PyPI maintainer account, vibiret, created on the attack date with permissions for the affected package and five related projects. However, the account’s direct involvement has not been verified. Impact and Response Organizations are urged to audit developer environments, CI/CD pipelines, and container images for the compromised versions. Affected installations should be replaced with verified packages, and potentially exposed credentials rotated. Suspicious cloud activity should be investigated, and impacted systems rebuilt. Security Recommendations Microsoft’s Agent Framework repository on GitHub is currently inaccessible, alongside several other Microsoft projects, though a connection to the incident remains unconfirmed. Security teams are advised to monitor for indicators of compromise, including unusual credential access patterns and unauthorized token generation. Broader Implications The incident highlights vulnerabilities in package distribution ecosystems and underscores the need for rigorous verification processes in software supply chains. Security teams are advised to monitor for indicators of compromise, including unusual credential access patterns and unauthorized token generation.

items.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
items.summary: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post . The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well. The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis . The code was disguised as diagnostics. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The stolen data went to a webhook.site address as compressed, encoded JSON. The attacker did not stop after the first release. While OX was researching the malware, version 1.26.1 was reverted to the clean 1.26.0. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security . Both were gone by about 21:20 UTC. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. The short window may not limit exposure. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. Container images, CI caches, and lockfiles built in the window could still contain it. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. No researcher has linked the two attacks. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. OX advised teams to check all environments, CI images, and lockfiles for either version and remove it. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.

The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm.

Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack.

Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

How the stealer worked

The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well.

The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps.

Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.

The code was disguised as diagnostics. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The stolen data went to a webhook.site address as compressed, encoded JSON.

The attacker did not stop after the first release. While OX was researching the malware, version 1.26.1 was reverted to the clean 1.26.0. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said.

The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. Both were gone by about 21:20 UTC.

Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened.

The short window may not limit exposure. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. Container images, CI caches, and lockfiles built in the window could still contain it.

OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access.

It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. No researcher has linked the two attacks.

What security teams should do

Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said.

OX advised teams to check all environments, CI images, and lockfiles for either version and remove it. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido.

items.title: Norwegian Gas Giant Equinor Says It’s Under Cyberattack. Production Keeps Running
items.summary: Norwegian Gas Giant Equinor confirms cyberattack on IT systems, with no impact on production or confirmed data theft. Equinor, Europe’s largest gas supplier, said on 17 November it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some IT systems. The Norwegian company said the attack had not affected operations and production, and it had taken steps to neutralise it. “Equinor has detected an ongoing cyber-attack against certain IT systems. Relevant resources have been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity.” reads the statement published by the company. “As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading. At present, there is no indication that the attack has consequences for employees, partners or suppliers. Production remains unaffected.” The energy giant said there was also no indication data had been stolen. A company spokesperson declined to give further details. The disruption reached everyday work, not the wells. Norwegian news agency NTB reported, citing the company, that IT applications and internal systems were affected, and a person at Equinor told Reuters the internal email system was down. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said it was aware of the attack and was ready to provide support if needed. Last month, the agency raised its cyber threat level to four on a five-level scale . It warned that cyberattacks could disrupt critical services such as water and electricity. NSM also reported that successful cyberattacks against Norwegian companies had tripled in the previous six months. “The incident currently being ⁠experienced ​by Equinor confirms that this risk ​is indeed high,” the NSM spokesperson said on Tuesday. This isn’t Norway’s first brush with this kind of pressure this year. In August, a pro-Russian group claimed a cyberattack that disrupted multiple Norwegian government digital services for several days. Separate claims from that period don’t establish who’s behind this week’s attack on Equinor, and nobody has named a group yet. Treat the gap between claim and evidence as the story for now. A company confirming an attack and ruling out operational impact is a fact; who did it and why is not, until someone shows proof. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Equinor)
