items.summary_html:
• Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643. 
  • The actor’s arsenal has several payloads including the Go-based Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), a Python-based infostealer internally labelled “Good Game,” and a multi-cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker. 
  • The threat actor is likely operating a campaign targeting cryptocurrency holders, gaming platform account owners, and VoIP software users based on the lure file names of the initial vectors and the payloads. 
  • The Overlord RAT implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos.
Victimology   

The threat actor is potentially targeting victims in Europe, according to the payload’s keyword-based file harvesting capability, which specifically targeted documents that had file names in English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese.  

Based on the lure themes and payload file names, the potential victim pool spans across multiple verticals. A lure financial statement decoy PDF — launched when the Good Game stealer is executed — indicates targeting finance and accounting staff. The Viber trojanized installer lure targets messaging platform users, while additional payload variants of files named microsip indicate targeting VoIP softphone operators, consistent with call-center or business telephone environments. Cryptocurrency and gaming users are also targeted by both the clipboard hijacker and the infostealer.  

Potential links to North Korea-aligned actors 

Talos assesses with low confidence that UAT-12643 is a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT) actor based on overlaps in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) with those of the other known North Korean APT actors.  

In the current campaign, Talos observed that the actor is using the Overlord RAT as one of their payloads. The threat cluster called UNK_DeadDrop, likely a North Korean threat actor, had employed the Overlord RAT in their earlier campaigns as reported by the security researchers in June 2026.  

The Overlord RAT variant observed in this campaign implements a blockchain C2 resilience technique with Solana blockchain transactions. This technique was first reported in March 2026, employed by the Lazarus APT group. Although the implementation methodology differs (earlier, it was through Node.js), the technique of leveraging Solana transaction memo stayed consistent.  

Talos is aware that Overlord RAT and Solana blockchain hosting technique is also leveraged by other threat actors in their campaigns, as reported by external security researchers in October 2026.  

Threat actor infrastructure 

Talos observed that the actor hosted the malicious files on a server with IP address “41[.]216[.]188[.]11”, running a Flask-based file delivery service on port 8000 with resumable byte-range download support, and serving the payload staging directory. Due to the actor’s operational security failure, the server’s root folder was exposed to the internet, and Talos’ analysis of the exposed folder showed us actor’s tool sets, and the port numbers configured on the C2 server for different services.  

Port number 

Service 

Payload file name 

8000 

Flask file-drop (HTTP) 

Payload.exe, MyApp2.exe, HTA files 

5173 

Overlord RAT WebSocket C2 

Ovl.exe, Client.exe  

5656 

Python stealer TCP C2 

Ova.exe, MyApp2.exe 

5959 

Python stealer TCP C2 

Microsip-config.exe, microsip-config1.exe 

The actor does not use the traditional data exfiltration approach of transferring the data to the C2 server; instead, the stolen data is exfiltrated using two different services. The actor used the discord webhook, which receives an immediate notification that contains a victim’s fingerprint and a single click download link. The stolen data archive is uploaded to “gofile[.]io” and is later accessed by the actor through the download link.  

We also observed the actor’s LNK generation script among the samples of the staging directory, indicating the actor’s lure creation workflow. The script accepts a payload URL and icon type (PDF, Word, or Windows Update) and generates a COM-based LNK with the spoofed and hidden execution.  

Figure 1. Sample Windows shortcut generation script.Initial access vectors 

Talos observed that the actor uses three different methods to gain initial access to victims’ environments. They have instrumented Windows shortcuts, HTA files, and XML files, so the embedded malicious instructions execute and grant initial access. In this campaign, we have not observed how the actor delivers these malicious initial vector files to victims’ machines.  

Weaponized LNK 

One of the initial access vectors is the usage of the weaponized LNK files paired with the icons spoofed from legitimate system binaries to appear as a legitimate file in the Windows Explorer.  

The shortcut file impersonates a PDF using the standard Windows document icon and abuses MpCmdRun.exe, Windows Defender's command line utility and the argument -DownloadFile to get the payload.  Since MpCmdRun.exe is a signed Microsoft binary, the download passes application allowlisting controls transparently. The downloaded payload will be saved as RuntimeBroker.exe to blend into process inventories, and the console window is minimized with no visible trace. 

Figure 2. Embedded command line in a sample LNK. 

Another shortcut file applies the same PDF disguise through a double-extension file name and the Microsoft Edge PDF icon and uses certutil -urlcache –f, a one-liner download command that operates under the guise of a certificate cache update. Both shortcuts were built on the same machine (win-8oa3ccqae4d). 

Figure 3. Embedded command line in a sample LNK. HTA dropper 

Talos observed that the actor has weaponized the JavaScript HTML Application (HTA) file to gain initial access. The weaponized HTA is executed by mshta.exe and the JavaScript in the HTA uses “MSXML2.ServerXMLHTTP” to fetch the payload as raw binary and “ADODB.Stream” to write it to %TEMP%\s.exe, then executes it stealthily by hiding the execution window. 

Figure 4. Sample HTA file.MSBuild living-off-the-land binary (LOLBin) 

The actor has also weaponized a standard MSBuild XML project file “dl.xml” by including an inline C# CodeTaskFactory task. When the XML file is executed via msbuild.exe, it compiles and executes the C# code in memory, and no intermediate executable is written to disk for the downloader stage. The download uses a spoofed Microsoft BITS/7.8 User-Agent string, impersonating the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) used by Windows Update, Microsoft Defender and many third-party updaters, so the request blends in with routine background download traffic. 

Figure 5. Sample malicious MSBuild project XML file. Analysis of Overlord RAT 

The Overlord RAT variant utilized by UAT-12643 in this campaign is a modular Windows RAT compiled from Go source code. 

The defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques implemented include the detection of in-memory execution to suppress forensic artifacts when running in sandboxes and a “kill flag” mechanism that triggers a kernel-level Blue Screen of Death (BSoD), making the process effectively unremovable without triggering a full system crash.  

The RAT first verifies that the current process is running with administrative privilege. It then acquires SeDebugPrivilege for the current process. With that privilege held, it calls a native NT kernel API (NtSetInformationProcess) directly, bypassing the documented Win32 API layer entirely, to set the ProcessBreakOnTermination information class on the current process handle to value 1, which indicates the kernel will handle the process as critical to system operation. With these settings, the operating system treats the process the same way as the core Windows system processes. When a user or a security tool attempt to forcibly terminate the process, the kernel does not allow it to exit cleanly. Instead, it immediately halts the entire operating system and triggers a BSoD with the stop code CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED.  

Figure 6. Snippet of Overlord RAT function that triggers BSoD.

For persistence, the RAT employs two approaches. The primary approach is through a registry autorun entry under the current user's hive, with a randomized value name pointing to the RAT binary located in the Network folder of the local user profile application data folder. The secondary approach is a pre-boot persistence via the Windows Recovery Environment OEM script path. It first removes any previous version of itself and then sets up the OEM environment directly under %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\. This folder is the location that the Windows Recovery Environment accesses when performing a "Reset this PC" operation. By placing files here, anything registered in this directory gets executed inside WinRE before the operating system is restored. 

Once the directory is set, the RAT generates a random 20-character file name for its payload file. Each character is picked individually at random from a fixed character set, meaning every installation produces a uniquely named file. With a random name chosen, it writes the RAT's own executable binary into the OEM directory as that payload file.  It then constructs the shell command that WinRE will use to launch the payload and wraps it into Windows batch script with the .bat extension. 

cmd.exe /c start %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\"random_stub_name"

The use of %TARGETOSDRIVE% is significant, as this environment variable only exists and resolves correctly inside the WinRE pre-boot environment, not in normal Windows. This means the command is specifically crafted to work at recovery time, not during a regular session.  

Before modifying any system configuration, it backs up the existing WinRE reset configuration file. Finally, it modifies the ResetConfig.xml file that governs what WinRE does during a reset. If no config file exists yet, it creates one from scratch; if one already exists, it patches it to append the malicious batch scripts as registered OEM tasks. From this point forward, whenever the victim triggers "Reset this PC" whether from within Windows Settings or from the recovery boot menu, Windows Recovery Environment will execute the RAT's payload before restoring the operating system, ensuring the implant survives a full system reset. 

Figure 7. Snippet of Overlord RAT function configuring the malicious script in WinRE location.

Analysis of the RAT’s binary showed a complete command surface with 35 commands, each corresponding to a distinct capability delivered over the C2 channel. These commands belong to several remote administration capability categories as described in the table below: 

Category 

Capabilities 

Surveillance 

Captures keystroke using GetAsyncKeyState, Webcam streaming, microphone and desktop audio capture and desktop screen capture. 

File system 

Directory listing and creation, file read, write, delete, copy, move, perform recursive search, upload, download, and compression tasks. 

Process control 

Process enumeration and termination. 

Script execution 

Execute arbitrary command and script with real-time console output streaming back to C2. 

Lateral Movement 

Establishes Reverse SOCKS proxy tunnel that routes operator TCP traffic through the victim network, enabling access to internal hosts unreachable from the public internet. 

Plugin delivery 

HTTP-based plugin downloads with reflective DLL injection at runtime where new capabilities are loaded entirely in memory with no binary update or written to the disk. 

Overlord’s Solana blockchain C2 URL hosting  

The RAT implements a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction. Any Solana wallet can include a memo instruction in a transaction of up to 566 bytes of arbitrary data to the permanent, globally replicated transaction record.  

Figure 8. The Snippet of Overlord RAT function queries the Solana Memo address.

A threat actor can post one such transaction from a controlled wallet address whenever the C2 server address needs to be updated. Every deployed RAT picks up the update on its next discovery cycle without any redeployment or reconfiguration.  

This is achieved by first retrieving the transaction history for the actor-controlled wallet using the Solana getSignatures JSON-RPC method which receives a chronologically ordered list of transaction signatures with the newest transaction first. For each signature it fetches the full transaction via getTransaction with jsonParsed encoding, which instructs the RPC node to decode every instruction data field into structured JSON response. The RAT module then walks every instruction in the parsed transaction looking for one whose data string is exactly 43 characters in length. The 43-character length is the fixed string length produced when a Base58-encoded WebSocket URL is AES-256 encrypted. Any instruction whose data field is a different length will be skipped, including legitimate Memo transactions from other users and all other Solana program instructions. Only instructions matching this precise length signature are treated as C2 memos.  

Figure 9. RPC response format for the getTransaction request. Good Game stealer 

The Good Game stealer payload Talos observed in the arsenal of UAT-12643 is a publicly available Python-based infostealer developed under the label "Good Game (version 1.1.2)” by CirqueiraDev. The actor of this campaign is not the developer, and the malware is distributed as a self-contained Windows executable produced by packaging a Python 3.12.0 code with PyInstaller. Its architecture is split between two cooperating bytecode modules. The “final_build.pyc” acts as the launcher, decoy interface, and reverse-shell client, while “kora.pyc” contains the full data-harvesting stealer logic. 

Good Game’s anti-analysis and evasion  

The malware employs evasion techniques at every stage of execution, beginning the moment the process starts. The launcher immediately retrieves the console window handle via GetConsoleWindow() and calls ShowWindow() to hide the terminal window. A fully functional Notepad-style graphical user interface (GUI) is rendered in the foreground via tkinter, a Python’s standard, built-in library used for creating GUIs while all malicious threads run as daemon threads behind it. 

Before the stealer module begins with any data collection, it runs three sequential execution checks. First, it confirms the host operating system is Windows by checking platform.system(); the stealer aborts silently on Linux or macOS. Second, it verifies network connectivity by performing an HTTP GET request to Google, and if the request fails, the stealer exits and records the failure reason in a file named “skipped" in the temporary directory. Third, and most significantly, it runs sandbox detection checks in five steps. 

  1. It checks for the presence of libraries including sbiedll.dll, api_log.dll, vmcheck.dll, wpespy.dll, cmdvrt64.dll, avghookx.dll, snxhk.dll, and guard32.dll.  
  2. The MAC address check extracts the host's network adapter hardware address via the getmac module and compares it against known OUI prefixes assigned to virtualization vendors: VMware (00:05:69, 00:0c:29, 00:50:56), VirtualBox (08:00:27), Hyper-V (00:15:5d), Xen (00:16:3e), and Parallels (00:1c:42).  
  3. The hardware memory check queries GlobalMemoryStatusEx through a ctypes MEMORYSTATUS structure and flags machines with less than two gigabytes of physical RAM as sandbox environments.  
  4. The boot-time check uses psutil.boot_time() to compute system uptime and treats an uptime of fewer than five minutes as indicative of a freshly provisioned analysis VM.  
  5. Finally, the Wine emulation check probes for the presence of “C:\windows\system32\wineboot.exe” to detect Windows API compatibility layers.  

If any single check triggers, the stealer exits silently, leaving no harvested data and minimal trace. 

The decoy URL mechanism of the stealer adds a further layer of camouflage. It opens a PDF-hosted document in the victim's default browser exactly once per machine and computes an MD5 hash of the URL and stores a flag file named “url_opened_.flag” in the temporary directory of the victim machine. On all subsequent executions, the lure URL is not re-opened, preventing repeated suspicious browser launches that would alert the victim. 

Figure 10. Decoy PDF opened by Good Game stealer in victim’s browser.Persistence established by Good Game 

The malware establishes persistence through two independent mechanisms on Windows, ensuring the implant survives reboots regardless of which pathway is disrupted. The primary method is a registry autorun by opening the key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run using winreg.KEY_SET_VALUE” and writes the absolute filesystem path of the running executable under the value name Zoipers, causing the binary to be launched automatically at every subsequent user logon without requiring elevated privileges. The secondary persistence mechanism is executed from within the stealer module of kora.pyc. The stealer copies the running executable into the Windows Startup folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ using shutil.copy().  

Beyond simple re-execution persistence, the stealer also temporarily disables the Windows Task Manager during its active operation. It calls advapi32.RegCreateKeyExW directly through ctypes against the key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System and sets a DWORD value DisableTaskMgr=1 via RegSetValueExW.  After the data exfiltration completes successfully, the stealer restores the value to zero (DisableTaskMgr=0), reducing the probability that the victim will notice the restriction. 

Good Game stealer functionalities  

The stealer's most extensive capability targets 23 Chromium-family and Firefox-based browser variants, covering Google Chrome across all distribution channels, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Opera GX, Brave, Vivaldi, Yandex Browser and all its regional variants, Amigo, Torch, Kometa, Orbitum, CentBrowser, 7Star, Sputnik, Epic Privacy Browser, Uran, and Iridium. 

The stealer scans LevelDB stores across Discord clients and over 19 Chromium-based browsers for authentication tokens using two regex patterns one for plain-text tokens and one for tokens encrypted with the “dQw4w9WgXcQ:” prefix introduced in newer Discord versions. It decrypts the stolen token via the browser's extracted master key, then validates each recovered token against the Discord API to build a complete account profile covering username, display name, user ID, email, phone number, Nitro subscription tier, linked payment methods, gift codes, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) status. 

The stealer additionally extracts ROBLOSECURITY cookies from browser databases, validating each against the Roblox authentication API to confirm active sessions and retrieve the associated account details. A full system profile is assembled covering hostname, username, hardware specifications, OS details, network interfaces, and public IP geolocation metadata queried from ipwhois.app, serialized to system_infos.txt in the archive root. 

The stealer also captures a full-monitor screenshot and a single webcam frame, both saved as PNGs and added to the archive before the temporary files are deleted and terminated. The stealer then harvests session data from 21 cryptocurrency wallets including Exodus, Electrum, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Atomic Wallet, Trust Wallet, Coinbase, and Binance, as well as four gaming platform launchers (Steam, Riot Games, Epic Games, and Rockstar Games).

items.title: 65 Characters to RCE: Inside the Java4Shell Vulnerability
items.summary: Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical OpenJDK Base64 bug enabling pre-auth RCE in Jenkins, Jira, Keycloak and more. Patches are out. Update now. Calif researchers disclosed Java4Shell, a memory-corruption bug, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score of 9.2), in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the world’s most common Java runtime. OpenJDK (Open Java Development Kit) is the open-source implementation of the Java platform. It provides the tools and components needed to develop and run Java applications, including the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), libraries and development tools. It is widely used in enterprise systems, servers and cloud environments. Base64 shows up everywhere: authentication, file uploads, network messages. To decode it fast, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 instructions that process many bytes at once, and the bug lives in that hand-written machine code. A single malformed string triggers it: 64 “A” characters followed by one equals sign, or 128 on older OpenJDK 17. The flaw sits in how the decoder handles padding at the end of a Base64 string. When the trailing characters are “=”, “==” or similar, the code can compute a negative output length, and that underflow turns into a write of all 64 bytes instead of the few that should go out. For a 65-character trigger, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte buffer and ends up writing 62 bytes past its end. “At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding . When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ( [64 bytes] + '=' ) as input, that calculation allocates a 50 -byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub , so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48 , an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.” reads the report published by Calif. “On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=' , because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.” Calif demonstrated that attackers could execute code remotely, without authentication, on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, all using their default settings. Applications built with Struts and Spring Boot were also vulnerable. A client-side attack could even target a Java program simply by making it connect to a malicious server over TLS. The attacker can initially control only where data is written, while most of the data itself is fixed. Calif bypassed this limitation using a technique often seen in browser attacks: corrupting the length of a nearby array so it can store attacker-controlled data. This turns a limited write operation into a much more powerful one. By applying the technique to another array, Calif also achieved the ability to read memory. This allows attackers to expose sensitive data from the Java process before executing code, a technique Calif calls JavaBleed. Getting two objects to land next to each other in memory took real engineering. Calif used a timing trick over the network, holding back parts of an HTTP request until earlier data was acknowledged, so it could control when the server allocated memory. They even rented a VM in the same region as the target, because a stable, low-latency connection matters more than clever TCP tuning. “For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration.” continues the report. “In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.” An AI coding assistant found the bug. Researcher Quang Luong pointed OpenAI’s Codex at OpenJDK’s internals and told it to audit the JIT compiler, intrinsics and cryptography, and most early results were useless. “It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit.” Calif states. “The total token cost was less than $200.” Total AI cost: under $200, which buys you a serious headache for a lot of enterprise software. There’s no universal exploit here. Every target needs its own delivery path, a writer, a reader and an application action, so a patch for one product doesn’t tell you about the next. Calif published a safe proof of concept that overwrites bytes inside a harmless array, and is holding back the weaponized chains until more systems are patched. Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, plus Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine and Red Hat OpenJDK. It also needs specific hardware: an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, found in Intel Xeon chips from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 systems are safe from this one. Oracle shipped a fix on 17 November as part of its November Critical Patch Update, which covers 655 vulnerabilities total. Update your Java runtime now. If you can’t patch immediately, start OpenJDK with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the accelerated decoder, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 hosts to turn off AVX-512, but treat both as a stopgap, not a fix. Calif frames the bigger problem as one of unused complexity: features built for a few applications ship to everyone, and everyone inherits the risk. “This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford. The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.” the report concludes. “With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?”” Below is a demo video of the exploits running published by Calif: Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical OpenJDK Base64 bug enabling pre-auth RCE in Jenkins, Jira, Keycloak and more. Patches are out. Update now.

Calif researchers disclosed Java4Shell, a memory-corruption bug, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score of 9.2), in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the world’s most common Java runtime. OpenJDK (Open Java Development Kit) is the open-source implementation of the Java platform. It provides the tools and components needed to develop and run Java applications, including the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), libraries and development tools. It is widely used in enterprise systems, servers and cloud environments.

Base64 shows up everywhere: authentication, file uploads, network messages. To decode it fast, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 instructions that process many bytes at once, and the bug lives in that hand-written machine code. A single malformed string triggers it: 64 “A” characters followed by one equals sign, or 128 on older OpenJDK 17.

The flaw sits in how the decoder handles padding at the end of a Base64 string. When the trailing characters are “=”, “==” or similar, the code can compute a negative output length, and that underflow turns into a write of all 64 bytes instead of the few that should go out. For a 65-character trigger, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte buffer and ends up writing 62 bytes past its end.

“At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.” reads the report published by Calif. “On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.”

Calif demonstrated that attackers could execute code remotely, without authentication, on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, all using their default settings. Remote code execution was also possible after authentication on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Applications built with Struts and Spring Boot were also vulnerable. A client-side attack could even target a Java program simply by making it connect to a malicious server over TLS.

The attacker can initially control only where data is written, while most of the data itself is fixed. Calif bypassed this limitation using a technique often seen in browser attacks: corrupting the length of a nearby array so it can store attacker-controlled data. This turns a limited write operation into a much more powerful one. By applying the technique to another array, Calif also achieved the ability to read memory. This allows attackers to expose sensitive data from the Java process before executing code, a technique Calif calls JavaBleed.

Calif used a timing trick over the network, holding back parts of an HTTP request until earlier data was acknowledged, so it could control when the server allocated memory. They even rented a VM in the same region as the target, because a stable, low-latency connection matters more than clever TCP tuning.

“For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration.” continues the report. “In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.”

An AI coding assistant found the bug. Researcher Quang Luong pointed OpenAI’s Codex at OpenJDK’s internals and told it to audit the JIT compiler, intrinsics and cryptography, and most early results were useless.

“It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit.” Calif states. “The total token cost was less than $200.”

Total AI cost: under $200, which buys you a serious headache for a lot of enterprise software.

There’s no universal exploit here. Every target needs its own delivery path, a writer, a reader and an application action, so a patch for one product doesn’t tell you about the next. Calif published a safe proof of concept that overwrites bytes inside a harmless array, and is holding back the weaponized chains until more systems are patched.

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, plus Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine and Red Hat OpenJDK. It also needs specific hardware: an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, found in Intel Xeon chips from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 systems are safe from this one.

Oracle shipped a fix on 17 November as part of its November Critical Patch Update, which covers 655 vulnerabilities total. Update your Java runtime now. If you can’t patch immediately, start OpenJDK with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the accelerated decoder, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 hosts to turn off AVX-512, but treat both as a stopgap, not a fix.

“This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.

The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.” the report concludes.

items.title: The resilience gap: Why cybersecurity investment alone is not enough
items.summary: Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality. Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong. Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing. Ultimately, the investment didn’t fail; the expectation did. Technology alone can’t deliver an outcome that also depends on people, process, governance and coordination. The lesson is clear: A well-funded cybersecurity program can still be operationally fragile. The findings in Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study illustrate the problem. Cybersecurity remains the leading strategic investment priority, selected by 48% of CISOs. Yet only 41% report high or very high confidence in their organizations’ ability to protect enterprise value, while just 29% express that level of confidence in responding with agility. Another 54% describe their confidence in their organizations’ ability to respond with agility as moderate. That gap should concern every CISO. It suggests organizations have built security capabilities without fully developing the enterprise operating model needed during disruption. The real test begins when prevention ends Security investment matters. But you aren’t buying away cyber risk. You’re buying it down. Even the most mature organizations will eventually face an event they cannot prevent, often involving a third party, technology failure or circumstance outside their control. What happens next separates resilient organizations from everyone else. Security works to contain the threat while infrastructure and application teams decide what can safely go offline. Business leaders push to restore critical services, sometimes with competing priorities. Legal weighs disclosure obligations with incomplete information. Communications prepares messages for employees, customers and regulators. Meanwhile, a cloud, software-as-a-service or other technology provider may control part of the environment the company needs to recover. That’s where resilience usually breaks down: not within any one team, but in the handoffs and decisions between them. In the exercises we run, the hardest questions are often surprisingly basic: Who has the authority to shut down a revenue-producing system? If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first? If Microsoft 365 or another primary collaboration platform is unavailable, how does the crisis team communicate? If a critical provider is also down, do its recovery priorities and timelines align with yours? The useful output of an exercise is not a reassuring score. It is the list of things that didn’t work: unclear authority, gaps in escalation paths, inaccessible backups and dependencies that teams incorrectly assumed had been tested. Consider Quantum Dawn VIII, SIFMA’s sector-wide exercise from November 2025 . The polycrisis scenario included an undersea cable cut, and roughly two-thirds of participants said they had either never tested that scenario or weren’t sure they had. That is exactly the kind of blind spot an exercise is designed to expose. Better to uncover it in an exercise than during an actual disruption. And the event you plan for is seldom the event you get. That’s why resilience cannot depend on following a script. Build a framework that enables collaboration and increases the speed of informed decisions, regardless of what actually happens. Cyber, AI and third-party risks no longer stay in their lanes Risks don’t arrive one at a time. A cyberattack can quickly become a privacy issue, a regulatory matter and a business interruption. A third-party outage becomes your outage. And AI can act as a force multiplier, allowing a single issue to move faster and spread across more data, systems and business processes. The findings support this. Cyber threats remain the highest-rated near-term concern in the Top Risks survey, but privacy, third-party risk, AI, resilience and regulatory uncertainty are now clustered closely behind. AI doesn’t change the fundamental resilience questions. It raises the stakes. An agent may read customer data, query an ERP system, act through a service account or trigger a workflow without a person clicking the button. So, start with an old question: What can it access? Then ask whose permissions or delegated authority it is using, what actions it can take, where those actions are logged and how quickly you can stop it when something goes wrong. CISOs appear to recognize that challenge. In our 2027 Top Risks study, 51% identified improving AI governance and accountability as a leading priority, while 45% pointed to workforce readiness. That’s telling. Sustainable adoption requires some basic discipline: maintain an inventory of agents and their owners, map the data and tools each can reach, restrict service accounts and delegated permissions, monitor actions and make sure access can be revoked quickly. Third parties deserve the same scrutiny. A third-party assessment can tell you a lot about a provider’s controls at a point in time. What it rarely tells you is how that provider will perform on a bad day. Most assessments still rely heavily on documentation, discussion and self-reporting. Those assessments may assure a provider’s security posture, but they do not prove that a critical service will remain available, that the provider’s recovery sequence aligns with yours or that the appropriate people on both sides know how to disconnect, communicate and restore service together. CISOs should be able to identify the external relationships most critical to business operations, understand the services and data that depend on them, and test what will happen if those relationships are interrupted. This broader responsibility is increasingly part of the CISO mandate. CSO’s examination of how CISOs can rise to the business resilience challenge describes the role’s evolution from a primarily preventive function toward greater responsibility for response, recovery and business resilience. Build resilience into the investments already underway If cyber risk increasingly travels through interconnected systems and infrastructure, resilience has to be part of how those environments are modernized in the first place. The percentage of CISOs selecting cybersecurity slipped from 53% to 48%, while the percentage selecting infrastructure modernization rose from 21% to 33%. Taken together, those shifts make sense. Security and modernization are increasingly intertwined. A cloud migration, enterprise resource planning (ERP) replacement, identity redesign or data-platform upgrade can retire unsupported systems and standing privileges. It can also create new concentration risk, recovery dependencies and failure points if resilience is not designed in from the start. CISOs should use these major transformation programs to improve resilience, not complicate it. Questions to ask include: Are we retiring legacy platforms and connections, or simply putting a new layer on top of them? Are old accounts, interfaces, backup jobs and vendor dependencies actually being removed? Can the order-to-cash, payments, customer service or other critical processes be restored faster after the investment? Are recovery, isolation and alternate-processing requirements in the architecture and acceptance criteria from the start? Have we tested the new platform’s recovery path, or are we assuming modernization made it more resilient? Closing the resilience gap The point isn’t to spend less on cybersecurity. It’s to expect more from the investment. The 2027 Top Risks study shows CISOs balancing cyber threats with AI, third-party risk, resilience and modernization. Those may look like separate priorities on a survey. In practice, they increasingly collide in the same incident. We aren’t going to prevent every cyber incident. The question is what happens when the next one gets through. Does the organization know what matters most, who makes the hard calls and how to recover? Or does it figure those things out during the crisis? That gap is the resilience gap. And it is where CISOs should be looking next.

CISOs should use these major transformation programs to improve resilience, not complicate it. Questions to ask include:

  • Are we retiring legacy platforms and connections, or simply putting a new layer on top of them?
  • Are old accounts, interfaces, backup jobs and vendor dependencies actually being removed?
  • Can the order-to-cash, payments, customer service or other critical processes be restored faster after the investment?
  • Are recovery, isolation and alternate-processing requirements in the architecture and acceptance criteria from the start?
  • Have we tested the new platform’s recovery path, or are we assuming modernization made it more resilient?
Closing the resilience gap

The point isn’t to spend less on cybersecurity. It’s to expect more from the investment. The 2027 Top Risks study shows CISOs balancing cyber threats with AI, third-party risk, resilience and modernization. Those may look like separate priorities on a survey. In practice, they increasingly collide in the same incident.

We aren’t going to prevent every cyber incident. The question is what happens when the next one gets through. Does the organization know what matters most, who makes the hard calls and how to recover? Or does it figure those things out during the crisis?

That gap is the resilience gap. And it is where CISOs should be looking next.

items.title: U.S. CISA adds Perforce Puppet Enterprise flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
items.summary: U.S. CISA adds Perforce Puppet Enterprise vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a Perforce Puppet Enterprise flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score of 9.4), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog . The critical vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 affects Puppet Server and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely on a vulnerable server. The flaw is caused by improper deserialization of untrusted data in Puppet’s report-processing component. The vulnerability can be exploited by a client holding a certificate signed by the Puppet Certificate Authority (CA). An attacker can send a specially crafted report through an HTTP PUT request to trigger the flaw and execute code with the privileges of the Puppet Server service account. This could give the attacker control over the server and potentially provide a path to compromise systems managed by the Puppet infrastructure. The risk is even greater when the CA automatically signs certificate requests without properly verifying them. In this configuration, an attacker with network access may be able to obtain a valid agent certificate without prior authentication and then exploit the vulnerability. As of the latest available vendor information, there are no reports confirming active exploitation of CVE-2026-115731. Perforce has stated that it is not aware of attacks exploiting the flaw and has found no evidence of customer data being accessed. No specific threat actor or campaign has been linked to this vulnerability. Perforce released security updates on November 3, 2026. Fixed versions include Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1 and 2023.8.13, and Puppet Core 9.1.3 and 8.22.2. Organizations should upgrade as soon as possible. Until then, they should disable automatic certificate signing unless requests undergo strong verification. According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities , FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog. Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure. CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by December 1st, 2026. The critical vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 affects Puppet Server and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely on a vulnerable server. The flaw is caused by improper deserialization of untrusted data in Puppet’s report-processing component.

The vulnerability can be exploited by a client holding a certificate signed by the Puppet Certificate Authority (CA). An attacker can send a specially crafted report through an HTTP PUT request to trigger the flaw and execute code with the privileges of the Puppet Server service account. This could give the attacker control over the server and potentially provide a path to compromise systems managed by the Puppet infrastructure.

The risk is even greater when the CA automatically signs certificate requests without properly verifying them. In this configuration, an attacker with network access may be able to obtain a valid agent certificate without prior authentication and then exploit the vulnerability.

As of the latest available vendor information, there are no reports confirming active exploitation of CVE-2026-115731. Perforce has stated that it is not aware of attacks exploiting the flaw and has found no evidence of customer data being accessed. No specific threat actor or campaign has been linked to this vulnerability.

Perforce released security updates on November 3, 2026. Fixed versions include Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1 and 2023.8.13, and Puppet Core 9.1.3 and 8.22.2. Organizations should upgrade as soon as possible. Until then, they should disable automatic certificate signing unless requests undergo strong verification.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by December 1st, 2026.

items.title: Codeberg.org Is Offline After Its Registrar Put the Domain on Hold, and a Forgejo Security Fix Is Stuck
items.summary: Codeberg.org, the non-profit code-hosting site many open-source projects use instead of GitHub, has been unreachable since early Wednesday morning. Its servers are running. Its name isn’t. The public registry record for codeberg.org shows a “client hold”, a status only the domain’s registrar can set, added at 05:52 UTC on 18 November. The registrar is NameSilo. Once DNS caches ran out, codeberg.org stopped resolving for everyone, and the first reports of that came in at about 07:20 UTC. Codeberg says the domain “entirely disappeared” from its NameSilo account. It didn’t forget to renew, it sees no suspicious logins, and the account’s domain history shows nothing. It also got no email warning it about a problem. A support ticket is open with NameSilo. The outage has a second victim. Forgejo, the software Codeberg runs and many others host on their own servers, had to stop a security release that was due today, after its patches had already been publicly visible for a while. Forgejo’s interim advice for self-hosters is in chapter 3. When we published, the outage was being discussed on Mastodon and Hacker News. We found no news coverage.

items.title: How organizations can secure their AI-generated code
items.summary: The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts. The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure. “He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit . “We’re EU based.” When asked whether he had read the AI-generated code or taken any security precautions, the new hire said, “My GitHub repo is private.” The IT manager took the concern to the CEO, who brushed it aside: “Let it go.” In many organizations, vibe coders build software without thinking much about security. Their apps may get the job done, but they are ticking bombs. In SusVibes , a benchmark of 186 real-world feature requests from open-source projects, agents given feature descriptions without security guidance produced working code up to 57% of the time. But only 11.8% of their solutions were secure. “The failures we saw were not careless errors,” says Danqing Wang of Carnegie Mellon University’s Language Technologies Institute, author of the paper describing SusVibes. “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do.” What has changed, especially this year, is that AI code-generating tools have gotten so good at producing working code that people are just trusting them, says Dr. Katie Paxton-Fear, staff security advocate at Semgrep. “Developers simply aren’t being as critical now as they were when AI was worse at writing code.” Whether it’s the vibe-coder in marketing or the seasoned engineering team boosting its productivity, AI-generated code is an increasing security concern for CISOs. Much of that is a function of volume, but even as AI has proved highly capable of finding flaws in code bases, it is not yet adept at contributing code without introducing its own . Treating AI-generated code as ‘untrusted input’ Leading AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Amazon Q Developer have become developer go-to tools, and CIOs are increasingly enlisting business users to vibe code their own apps . But as AI-generated code surfaces everywhere, CISOs have only one option: to treat it “as untrusted input that has to earn its way into the codebase,” says Bianca Lankford, VP of engineering at Datadog. To do so, security leaders are moving security checks closer to where code is written: static analysis, secrets scanning, and dependency checks run on every pull request and, increasingly, in the developer’s editor. “Companies are also approving specific AI tools, limiting what assistants can access, and training reviewers to spot common AI mistakes like outdated libraries, weak input validation, and overly permissive defaults,” Lankford adds. At Mimecast, using AI to write code doesn’t remove the developer’s responsibility for it, says Leslie Nielson, CISO at the information security vendor. “A named person owns every AI-assisted change that ships, and that’s recorded in the pull request, not assumed,” he adds. “AI can propose. Only people can approve.” The volume of code organizations need to review is only growing, and reviewing everything manually can be impossible. That’s why Nielsen recommends security leaders combine automated checks with human judgment. “We use automation for the known and repetitive, like dependency checks, secrets detection, and standard vulnerability patterns,” he says. “We keep a person accountable for anything involving access, authentication, or sensitive data. Those categories always go to a specialist reviewer, regardless of how clean the scan looks.” Datadog’s Lankford says the decision to bring in a specialist should depend on what the code could put at risk, not on what entity — human or AI — wrote it. “Anything involving authentication, cryptography, payments, personal data, or infrastructure goes to a specialist, and code owner rules can route those changes automatically,” she says. “Other useful signals include diff size, new dependencies, and changes to permissions or network exposure.” The goal is to protect the human reviewers’ attention. “A reviewer buried in low-risk changes isn’t reviewing,” Nielsen adds. “They’re approving.” Another priority should be preserving the knowledge behind the code. “Generative AI may produce software, but it cannot produce understanding,” notes Alex Ștefănescu, security expert and tech activist. “Documentation, a solid test suite, and a written record of every significant architecture decision ever made are going to save developers and organizations countless hours when a security incident hits or when they are debugging complex issues.” All of this should be created and maintained by people and intended for human use, not externalized to generative algorithms, Ștefănescu adds. What’s at risk with AI-generated code The inclusion of third-party libraries or phantom dependencies — dependencies that are not explicitly declared in a manifest file — is a common concern with AI-generated code, as these unreported software packages might not be identified during a scan and can potentially hide vulnerabilities. One way to address this is to use software composition analysis (SCA) and software supply chain security tools to help identify the libraries in use, as well as the vulnerabilities and potential legal and compliance issues that might bring. While not unique to AI-generated code, organizations also expose themselves to risks when developers download machine learning (ML) models or datasets from platforms such as Hugging Face. “In spite of security checks on both ends, it may still happen that the model contains a backdoor that becomes active once the model is integrated,” says Ștefănescu. “This could ultimately lead to data being leaked from the company that used the malicious models.” When it comes to coding agents and code completion functionality in tools like GitHub Copilot, Ștefănescu worries about hallucinations. “An LLM will always generate the most statistically probable continuation of a given prompt, so there are no real guarantees in place that it will generate a real package from PyPI, for example, after the word ‘import’,” they say. “Some attackers are aware of this and register package names on platforms like npm and PyPI, filling in some functionality that code completion tools suggest in order to make the packages seem legitimate.” If these packages are imported into real applications, they can do real damage. Sensitive information inadvertently leaking into codebases because of developers using AI-powered coding tools is another key concern. To address these risks, CISOs can establish protocols for downloading and integrating ML models or datasets from external platforms such as Hugging Face and ensure those protocols are incorporated in AI code agents’ instruction files where applicable. Such protocols can include implementing automated scanning tools to detect malicious code or backdoors, having a policy that only allows the use of models from verified publishers, or conducting internal testing in isolated environments. Not all AI-based code comes from teams full of software engineers. “We see a lot of adoption being driven by data analysts, marketing teams, researchers, etc., within organizations,” says Darren Meyer, staff research engineer at Endor Labs. These teams aren’t traditionally developing their own software but are increasingly writing simple tools that adopt AI libraries and models, so they’re often not aware of the risks involved. “This combination of shadow engineering with lower-than-average application security awareness can be a breeding ground for risk,” he adds. To make sure these teams are working safely, CISOs must consider forming relationships with these teams early in the process. Cybersecurity leaders might also want to set up training programs tailored to non-traditional development teams to educate data analysts, marketing professionals, and researchers on the potential risks associated with AI-based tools and libraries. Investing in defense “Security budgets don’t generally grow at the same pace that software development accelerates, and AI adoption is only widening that gap,” Meyer says. Application security is often underfunded in most organizations, yet allocating sufficient time and resources to it is essential, as AI adoption and AI-assisted coding accelerate the pace of software development. “A portfolio of high-quality security tools that can help address this gap is no longer optional,” Meyer says. “And while tools are critical to closing the gap, so are AppSec and ProdSec staff that can effectively partner with developers — even non-traditional developers — and understand the technical, compliance, and security implications of AI.” When it comes to securing enough resources to protect AI systems, some stakeholders might hesitate, viewing it as an optional expense rather than a critical investment. “AI adoption is a divisive topic in many organizations, with some leaders and teams being ‘all-in’ on adoption and some being strongly resistant,” Meyer says. “This tension can present challenges for insightful CISOs and business information security officers (BISOs).” CISOs that are aware of both the advantages and disadvantages of this might try to set controls to manage risks effectively, but this might create the perception of holding the organization back from innovating if they don’t explain what they do properly. “Organizations need to develop comprehensive strategies that balance the productivity benefits of AI tools with robust security practices,” says Thomas Segura, senior technical writer at GitGuardian. Cost-effective changes CISOs should implement But if a security leader has 90 days and no budget to spare, which changes would have the biggest impact? Datadog’s Lankford says a short, plain-language AI tool policy can make expectations clear. At a minimum, such a policy should spell out which tools employees can use, what code and data they can share, and which changes need specialist review. The aim is to give people answers they can use while they work, with a clear point of contact when they’re unsure. It’s also important to understand that employees don’t want to circumvent policies. They just want to get their work done without friction and without waiting weeks for approval. Giving them the right tools makes the safer route easier to take. By contrast, banning tools doesn’t work, because employees will find a way to still use them. A ban can push AI use out of sight, leaving security teams with less visibility into the code being written and the data being shared, Mimecast’s Nielsen says. CISOs should look across the development process to identify where they can intervene and which risks they can address at each stage. “Understand what layers you can influence and what vulnerabilities you can influence at each layer: in the design phase, in the CLAUDE.md file, as the agent is writing, during a pull request, as part of an AI pentest,” Semgrep’s Paxton-Fead says. It’s also important to explain to employees who are using AI code-generating tools that security lives in an implicit context: the threat model, the trust boundaries, what the attacker controls. “Agents cannot reliably plan and reason on these, so they optimize for the only signal they have, which is to satisfy the given functionality description,” Carnegie Mellon’s Wang says. When things go wrong, people in the organization need to feel safe telling security what happened, including which unapproved tools they used and what data they shared. Fear of punishment can delay that conversation, leaving the team trying to contain a problem without the full picture. “Offer amnesty instead of a crackdown, so people tell you the truth about what they’re using,” Nielsen advises.

items.title: The forced audit: how AuditTeam’s OpsAgent framework masks ransomware as consulting
items.summary: AuditTeam is an active threat group that uses the OpsAgent framework to compromise organizations across at least seven countries and territories. The campaign began in January 2026 and remained active through October 2026, at a minimum. In its ransom note, AuditTeam demands an “Audit & Consulting fee” in exchange for vulnerability reports. During this period, the group has infected dozens of organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also claims victims in seven additional countries. OpsAgent provides file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture, and network pivoting. During the campaign OpsAgent was transitioned from C++ to Rust while adding new capabilities including interactive shells and WebSocket upgrades. Its command-and-control domains use Amazon CloudFront subdomains, which OpsAgent discovers via a public GitHub repository. Two specialized modules extend its functionality. An antivirus/endpoint detection and response (AV/EDR) killer module installs a digitally signed Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus driver to terminate security products. A cryptor module encrypts files using AES-CBC or ChaCha20 with X25519 key exchange and targets database processes for termination prior to doing so. Background On March 10, 2026, we discovered suspicious activity targeting an organization in Hong Kong. The tool used was OpsAgent, a framework designed to resemble a penetration testing utility. Further investigation revealed attacks in additional countries, prompting an active research phase. This implant offers extensive operator capabilities, including host reconnaissance, shellcode injection via named pipes, and lateral movement through agent networks based on compromised hosts. Analysis indicates OpsAgent was used by AuditTeam. The group was first mentioned publicly by dbdigest.com in March 2026. On June 25, 2026, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam had claimed responsibility for an attack on a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. AuditTeam leaves a ransom note threatening to release stolen data unless a fee is paid. They call this fee the “Audit & Consulting fee.” According to the note, payment results in a vulnerability report being delivered to the victim instead of leaking the stolen data archive to the public internet. While the note does not mention file encryption, it is left by the cryptor module. Therefore, if a victim sees the note, their files are already encrypted. The ransom note GitHub commit history shows the campaign started on January 5, 2026. The leak site lists its first victim on February 21, 2026. Dozens of machines across at least seven countries were infected. On August 19, 2026, a C2 domain for the new OpsAgent version was added to the public repository and subsequently used in attacks. AuditTeam activity timeline Technical details Loaders OpsAgent uses multiple loader variants during its campaign. All discovered loaders unpack OpsAgent by parsing the MZ header and transferring execution to the entry point of the unpacked payload. The C loader was discovered in April 2026. It injects shellcode into msiexec.exe using standard API calls: CreateProcessA , VirtualAllocEx , WriteProcessMemory , and CreateRemoteThread . The .NET loader was found in June 2026. It uses NtQueueApcThread instead of direct process creation for injection. It contains strings such as DApc , DProtect , DResume , and msiexec.exe . Both the C and .NET loaders inject shellcode into a separate target process. They are also protected by OLLVM obfuscation with control-flow flattening enabled. In September 2026, we discovered the Rust loader. It retrieves an encrypted payload from the C2 server, decrypts it, parses the PE header, and runs the Execute export function within its own process rather than injecting into another process. This in-process execution model eliminates the need for remote process manipulation. OpsAgent main implant The implant (version 5.2.8) rivals Cobalt Strike in functionality. It uses a worker-thread architecture: the main thread monitors connection health, while a worker thread processes commands from a queue. Three concepts structure its behavior: the worker thread (handles nearly all C2 commands) jobs (background tasks run in separate processes) links (connections to child agents used for lateral movement) Exceptions include info , jobs , jobkill , worker_status , worker_restart , and exit , which execute immediately in the main thread. OpsAgent can optionally obtain its C2 address by reading a public GitHub repository: hxxps://github[.]com/RonaldCMalcolm1983/staticPage . The address is stored in an encrypted form using AES‑CBC with the SHA‑256 hash of f4bb8c7e15d8b98d535eb20b09176b3d as the key and a zero initialization vector. The encrypted payload is wrapped with the markers GetConfig and EndConfig and then base64‑encoded. Several commands — mimikatz_spawn , execute_assembly , pth_spawn , runpe , monitor start , and screenshot_service start — run background jobs in a separate process. To run a job, each creates a process and a named pipe, and receives shellcode from the C2 server. No command contains embedded mimikatz or PTH binaries. All payloads arrive remotely through the pipe, encrypted with XOR using key 604902af7b70b271 . By default these commands use msiexec.exe as a host process, but the path can be changed. The exception is the monitor command, which uses notepad.exe for shellcode injection. This design keeps the implant small and lets operators deliver custom payloads remotely. Injection commands support two modes: Legacy and DbgInjector. Legacy mode uses CreateProcessA and NtCreateThreadEx . DbgInjector creates a process in DEBUG state, allocates shared memory, sets a hardware breakpoint on FileTimeToSystemTime , then redirects RIP to the shellcode without creating a new thread. Several code patterns suggest LLM-assisted development. For example, OpsAgent resolves WinAPI functions dynamically by hash: it calculates the hash of a function name, then searches for the matching address. Sometimes the plaintext name remains in memory before hashing. Additionally, all injection commands share near‑identical code structures, differing only in argument count and target process selection. This uniform approach matches LLM‑generated scaffolding. Commands description The OpsAgent command set covers file system operations, process management, privilege escalation, shellcode injection, monitoring, and network pivoting. The C2 protocol runs over WebSocket with TLS and exchanges data in units called frames. Protocol frame types function as an extra command set enabling SOCKS proxy establishment, chunked file uploads, and inter-agent data forwarding. These frames are handled by a dedicated frame-handler function rather than the standard command decoder. The following combined table lists all text-based commands and protocol frame types together. Several commands deserve closer attention. The monitor command manages keylogging through subcommands that start, stop, and configure logging threads. Screenshot features follow a similar design with session management subcommands. In contrast, the pivot subsystem uses a flatter command structure where each pivot command ( pivot_list , pivot_start , pivot_stop , pivot_add , pivot_remove , pivot_auto ) operates independently without nested subcommand hierarchies. Some frame type numbers such as 0x20 appear unused in the current implementation. These may be traces of previous versions. SOCKS connection Frame type 0x44 Control SOCKS connections Frame type 0x52 Forward frame to child agent Frame type 0x54 Close link connection Additional modules AV/EDR killer module This module installs a driver disguised as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus (KV series), utilizing the \KvCorePortX0 filter port for communication. Upon receiving the 0x1D command followed by a target filename, the driver terminates the corresponding process. Its target list covers nearly every major security product on the market. Additionally, the driver carries a valid digital signature, which facilitates its initial execution. The process kill list contains approximately 220 entries, including: Security products: MsMpEng , SecurityHealthService , avp , ekrn , ccSvcHst , fcag , eadrline Remote access tools: TeamViewer_Desktop , TeamViewer_Service , tv_w32 , tv_x64 Monitoring/logging: Sysmon , Sysmon64 , splunkd , wazuh-agent Backup services: VeeamNFSSvc , AcronisAgent , MBAMService Database processes: sqlservr , mysqld , mongod , redis-server Cryptor module This module encrypts files using either AES-CBC or ChaCha20 based on a command-line flag. Each file receives a unique encryption key produced by RtlGenRandom . A 12-byte array serves as the ChaCha20 nonce or expands to a 16-byte AES initialization vector. Key exchange relies on X25519 Diffie-Hellman with a static public key embedded in the binary. The module generates an ephemeral key pair per session and encrypts the file key with ChaCha20 using the shared secret. Beyond file encryption, the module actively disrupts infrastructure by terminating database processes including SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. It also stops backup services such as Veeam. The module removes shadow copies, empties the recycle bin, and wipes temporary folders. Furthermore, any file deletion overwrites content with random data before removing the entry, preventing forensic recovery. After encryption, the module drops a ransom note. It formats the message as an audit log demanding payment through a Tor onion address. The note offers two options: pay the “Audit & Consulting fee” for a vulnerability report or face public data disclosure. Finally, the module’s configuration parameters include file extensions to encrypt, directories and files to whitelist, processes and services to terminate, and shadow copy deletion flags. OpsAgent-rs (Rust version) The Rust rewrite maintains functional parity with the C++ version while introducing new capabilities. OpsAgent-rs initially communicates with the C2 via HTTP POST requests to retrieve commands. There are special commands that change this behavior. After receiving an upgrade command, the implant establishes a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS for ongoing C2 communication instead of continuing to send POST requests. Additionally, command identifiers shifted from text names to numeric constants. New commands include interactive shells, directory creation, and sleep-interval changes. Command mapping between versions shows most legacy commands have Rust equivalents. However, screenshot and monitor commands now consolidate into a unified identifier rather than relying on an extensive set of subcommands. The Rust version removes the entire pivot command set, eliminating pivoting task management functionality. C2 acquisition in the Rust version changed significantly. The configuration contains a flag controlling whether the implant checks GitHub for new C2 addresses. It also stores markers indicating the beginning and end of the encrypted C2 string. The GitHub README page holds both the legacy C2 format and an additional base64-encoded blob specifically for OpsAgent-rs. The encryption scheme was reworked to use AES-GCM instead of AES-CBC. To derive the GCM key, the decryption flow computes HMAC-SHA256 of the secret key c2-framework-psk-salt-v1 against the configuration data blob, then applies a second HMAC with the salt c2-encryption-key\x01 . The nonce is the first 12 bytes of the decrypted payload and the tag occupies the last 16 bytes. Infrastructure The implant uses AWS-generated CloudFront CDN subdomains as C2 endpoints. Because these domains operate on shared infrastructure, their underlying IP addresses cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs. Domain IP Added on GitHub First seen ASN d19v1tntmz2i98.cloudfront.net – Jan 29, 2026 Feb 21, 2026 – d35htktbyt7nxc.cloudfront.net – Aug 20, 2026 Sep 6, 2026 – – 157.20.104.111 Aug 19, 2026 Aug 24, 2026 AS 136557 The GitHub repository stayed active throughout the campaign until November 2026. Commit history shows ongoing updates until September 29, 2026, when the actor removed the legacy C2 domain from the repository. This suggests the actor maintains the infrastructure actively and rotates domains as needed. In November 2026, the GitHub repository was removed. However, this does not mean the campaign is over, as the latest Rust implants found contained a configuration with the GitHub feature disabled. Victims AuditTeam targets organizations from different countries. We observed victims in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia. And according to the group’s leak site, there are victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan, and Spain. All identified victims belong to different industries. Attribution We attribute the OpsAgent campaign to AuditTeam with high confidence. The following evidence supports this assessment: Ransom note format and “Audit & Consulting fee” terminology unique to this group Tor-based leak site listing targeted organizations Operational philosophy distinguishing them from conventional ransomware groups through remediation reports Open sources first identified AuditTeam in March 2026 via dbdigest.com . In June, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam claimed responsibility for attacking a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. The group claims a mission to educate organizations about cybersecurity through exploitation and remediation reports. This tactical approach separates them from traditional ransomware operators. Conclusions AuditTeam frames extortion as a paid security audit — a distinctive model among ransomware groups. The C++ to Rust transition signals continued toolchain investment. New Rust commands cover interactive shells, WebSocket upgrades, and directory management. The specialized modules reveal thorough operational preparation: the AV/EDR killer uses a signed Jiangmin driver to disable security products, and the cryptor module terminates database processes, encrypts files, and removes shadow copies. These tools let the group neutralize defenses and optionally destroy data. CloudFront CDN subdomains complicate takedown and make IP-based blocking impractical because the IP space is shared with legitimate traffic. While the actor rotates infrastructure, the public GitHub repository enables C2 discovery and its removal disrupts the attack chain. Custom malware frameworks are typically developed and maintained by APT groups with dedicated engineering resources. AuditTeam shows that a ransomware crew can build comparable tooling. This shift may be enabled by AI-assisted development tools lowering the barrier to creating functional, multi-module implant architectures.
